Hence, pipeline components making outbound service requests require their own (non-human) client identity. This is true in particular for the custom CSV client, which periodically pulls data from SAP IDM.

In more conventional scenarios where IDM CSV Server is accessed from an on premises CSV client, HTTP basic authentication is the only available option. That’s not a secure choice for public cloud scenarios, however. It’s a better practice to use modern, secure authentication methods and hide SAP system internals, such as the credentials of SAP NetWeaver AS Java service users, from public cloud clients altogether. To this end, we’re going to build an API proxy in SAP API Management that requires clients to present an OAuth access token to be granted access to IDM CSV Server. OAuth 2.0, specifically its client credentials grant type, provides a secure and modern framework that enables clients in machine-to-machine scenarios to access protected resources on their own behalf - rather than on behalf of any specific human user. Without loss of generality, we’ll assume that the OAuth authorization server required by this architecture is provided by Microsoft Entra ID.

A Closer Look at Authentication and Authorization

The OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant type begins with the custom CSV client sending its client ID and client secret to the OAuth authorization server, in our case Microsoft Entra ID. In response to successful authentication, Entra ID returns an access token, which is a JSON Web Token (JWT). The CSV client then performs a second HTTP request, this time to the custom API proxy hosted in SAP API Management. The client sends the JWT received from Entra ID along with its HTTP request to the API proxy.

The API proxy verifies the JWT using a JSON Web Key (JWK), which it must fetch from Entra ID first. By verifying the JWT’s digital signature using the JWK, the API proxy confirms that the claims contained in the JWT can be trusted. After validating basic claims such as issuer and audience, the API proxy uses an additional claim (called “roles”) from the JWT to check whether this particular client is authorized to call IDM CSV Server. The rationale is to prevent that any authenticated client in possession of a valid access token from the trusted issuer is implicitly granted access to IDM CSV Server. Only clients explicitly authorized for this resource shall be granted access.

If the API proxy’s claims-based authorization check is successful, it sends a new, separate HTTP request to SAP Cloud Connector on premises, which in turn forwards that to the SAP NetWeaver AS Java backend. The API proxy does not forward the CSV client’s JWT in its own HTTP call. Instead, it uses HTTP basic authentication under the caller identity of a separate service user. This service user, which is managed by SAP NetWeaver AS Java, has been configured statically in SAP API Management at deployment time of the API proxy. Hence, there’s an identity context switch taking place in the API proxy at runtime - all calls to the backend or target endpoint will be made under one single caller identity. This switch to a pre-configured, static identity effectively cancels out IDM CSV Server’s built-in access control - all calls from API proxy to backend will be granted access. That’s why the API proxy needs its own, additional layer of authentication and authorization based on OAuth 2.0 on its front end side or proxy endpoint, as illustrated before.

Hands-On: Configuration Tasks in Microsoft Entra ID

Creating App Registrations in Microsoft Entra ID

We will create two app registrations for our scenario:

  1. One for the server side component providing protected resources, i.e. for IDM CSV Server
  2. One for the client side component requesting access to these resources, i.e. for the custom CSV client

To complete the following steps in your Microsoft Entra ID tenant, you’ll need authorized access to the Microsoft Entra Admin Center at

https://entra.microsoft.com

Your Entra ID user needs at least directory role Application Developer.

Creating the App Registration for the Server

Let’s start with the app registration for the server side. Navigate to Entra ID > App Registrations and use the New registration button.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: New app registration for idm-csv-server

Provide a name, such as idm-csv-server, for the new app registration. Note that these names are not unique - there can be many app registrations with the same name. Leave Supported account types at its default Single tenant only. Do not provide any redirect URI. Use the Register button to save the app registration.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Save app registration for idm-csv-server

Adding an Application ID URI to the Server’s App Registration

The second step is to create an OAuth resource identifier, or application ID URI in Entra ID terms. This will be needed at runtime, first by the CSV client when requesting an access token from Entra ID for a specific scope, and subsequently by the API proxy in SAP API Management to validate the audience claim contained in the access token.

To create an application ID URI, find the entry Add an Application ID URI on the app registration’s Overview form or navigate to Entra ID > App registrations > idm-csv-server > Expose an API.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add application ID URI for idm-csv-server

Use the Add button on the subsequent form Expose an API:

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add application ID URI for idm-csv-server > Add

This will open the Edit application ID URI form, which will display the default application ID URI for this app registration. In Entra ID, the default value is api://<application (client) ID>, where application (client) ID is a GUID unique to this app registration.

GUIDs are hard to remember, so it might be tempting to change the default and define a custom application ID URI, such as api://idm-csv-server. I recommend you don’t do this, however.

Microsoft defines pretty strict syntax rules for application ID URIs, which are documented at https://aka.ms/identifier-uri-formatting-error. Unfortunately, easy to remember values like api://idm-csv-server don’t comply with these rules. Hence, I recommend staying with the default value. Before using the Save button, copy the application ID URI into the clipboard and save it locally for later use.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add application ID URI for idm-csv-server > Save

You’ll need the application ID URI of idm-csv-server when working through the companion tutorial at two distinct points:

  1. in SAP API Management for configuring the API proxy after deployment using Key Value Maps (KVMs). The application ID URI of idm-csv-server goes into key jwtAudience of KVM IDM_CSV_SERVER_CONFIG.
  2. after completing deployment and configuration in SAP API Management for testing the integration scenario end-to-end. The application ID URI of idm-csv-server is part of the required value for IDM CSV Server Linux client’s command line parameter --oauth-scope.

Defining an App Role for the Server

Navigate to Entra ID > App Registrations > idm-csv-server > App roles and use the Create app role button.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Create app role for idm-csv-server

On the Create app role form, enter a descriptive role name. Since this role, although defined by the server, is supposed to be assigned to the client, CSV Client is a suitable display name.

In the Allowed member types section, choose Applications. This is important because it is a prerequisite to be able to assign this app role to the second app registration for the client, which we will create shortly.

The string you enter in the third field, Value, is significant for authorization checks at runtime and hence by far the most important. The convention for app role values in Entra ID is <Resource>.<Operation>. For the server’s app registration, I recommend that you enter the following, case-sensitive string exactly as shown here:

 

IdmCsvServer.Invoke

It is this exact string that Entra ID will put into the roles claim of the access token. For a positive authorization decision, the string maintained here must be equal to what the API proxy in SAP API Management checks at runtime to decide whether the client is authorized to use IDM CSV Server or not.

Finally, enter something meaningful for the mandatory Description field and make sure to keep Do you want to enable this app role? checked, then use Apply to save your changes.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Maintain app role value

Note that it is possible -although rarely required- to customize the app role value to something else. Keep in mind, however, that the app role value defined here, and the value checked in SAP API Management at runtime must match. Hence, if you decide to customize the app role value to something else here in Entra ID, make sure to also customize KVM key jwtClaimValue in SAP API Management to exactly the same value.

Creating the App Registration for the Client

Our next task is to create a second app registration, this time for the CSV client. While similar to what we have just done for the server, the procedure for the client differs significantly in two key aspects:

  1. Contrary to the server’s, the client’s app registration will require a client secret, enabling the client to authenticate with Entra ID at runtime - something the server never needs to do.
  2. Instead of defining a new app role, we’ll assign the server’s existing app role to the client’s app registration, thereby authorizing the client to invoke the server’s API.

Navigate to Entra ID > App Registrations and use the New registration button. Use idm-csv-client as display name for this app registration.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: New app registration for idm-csv-client

Just as you did earlier for the server, leave Supported account types at its default Single tenant only and do not provide any redirect URI. Use the Register button to save the app registration.

Adding a Client Secret to the Client’s App Registration

To create a client secret, find the entry Add a certificate or secret on the app registration’s Overview form or navigate to Entra ID > App registrations > idm-csv-client > Certificates & secrets.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add client secret to idm-csv-server

Use the New client secret button on tab Client secrets of the subsequent form Certificates & secrets:

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add client secret to idm-csv-client > New

Provide a description and expiration period for the client secret, then use Add to save your changes. Note that Entra ID’s default expiration period of six months might be significantly longer than what most organizations will realistically need for migrating their data from SAP IDM to NextGen IAM, so it’s worth considering a shorter expiration period here.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add client secret to idm-csv-client > Save

Before pressing the Add button, make sure you have figured out a secure location, such as a vault or password manager, where to store the secret’s clear text value that will be displayed in the next step - recovering the cleartext value later on is not possible.

At runtime, the custom CSV client contained in the migration pipeline will need the combination of this client secret and the application (client) ID, which we’ll take care of next, to authenticate with Entra ID and obtain an access token. You’ll also need these values at the end of the companion tutorial to perform end-to-end tests.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Add client secret to idm-csv-client > Copy

To obtain the application (client) ID, navigate back to this app registration’s Overview or alternatively Entra ID > App registrations > idm-csv-client > Overview. Find the entry called Application (client) ID and save that to your vault/password manager alongside the client secret saved earlier.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Copy client ID of idm-csv-client

Configuring Permissions of the Client’s App Registration

During creation of the server’s app registration, we defined a new app role whose value was IdmCsvServer.Invoke. Now we’ll assign this app role to the client’s app registration. OAuth distinguishes between delegated permissions for applications acting on behalf of a signed-in user and application permissions for applications acting on their own behalf. We’re discussing a machine-to-machine scenario here, so no signed-in user exists and delegated permissions are irrelevant. We’ll remove any delegated permissions which the client app registration got by Entra ID’s default, and assign IdmCsvServer.Invoke as application permission instead.

As we’ll see, this application permission assignment requires a two-step process: an application developer requests the assignment, and an application administrator approves or consents to, in OAuth terms, the assignment.

Removing Delegated Permissions from the Client’s App Registration

As stated above, our application doesn’t need any delegated permissions. However, every new app registration in Entra ID gets the delegated permission User.Read for Microsoft Graph API by default. While this doesn’t hurt our client from a functional perspective, we’ll remove the unneeded permission anyway on the grounds of principle of least privilege (PoLP).

Navigate to Entra ID > App registrations > idm-csv-server > API permissions.

In the Configured permissions section, verify that idm-csv-client currently has User.Read from category Microsoft Graph. Use the button labeled with three dots next to that category and select the Remove all permissions menu entry. The CSV client doesn’t use Microsoft Graph API at all, so we can safely remove all related permissions.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Remove delegated permission from idm-csv-client

Confirm the warning message claiming that these delegated permissions are required for proper application functionality - in our case, they are not. Use Yes, remove to apply your changes.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Confirm remove delegated permission from idm-csv-client

Requesting Application Permissions for the Client’s App Registration

Continue on the same form API permissions of idm-csv-client where you left off in the previous section and use Add a permission.

This will open a new form Request API permissions. Select the My APIs tab. In the list of applications displayed on this tab, find idm-csv-server - the server’s app registration which defines the permission we intend to assign to the client.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Expand API permissions defined by idm-csv-server

Click on idm-csv-server to display all API permissions (or app roles) defined by the server. Check the box next to IdmCsvServer.Invoke, then use Add permissions to apply your changes.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Request API permission defined by idm-csv-server for assignment to idm-csv-client

Verify that IdmCsvServer.Invoke is now being listed under Configured permissions and that its status is shown as Not granted for <your Entra ID tenant name>. Fixing this status is what we’ll take care of next.

Granting Admin Consent for the Requested Application Permissions: Prerequisites

As explained earlier, M2M scenarios cannot use interactive permission request and consent at runtime because there’s no signed-in user. Hence, consenting to permission requests is something a dedicated application administrator must do before the application can successfully execute. This application administrator will need to consent to this permission request not only for himself or any specific end user, but rather for all users - in other words, for the complete Entra ID tenant. Giving such administrative approval is what is commonly referred to as granting admin consent in OAuth terms.

If you’ve followed my instructions verbatim and currently use the Microsoft Entra Admin Center as a user who merely has directory role Application Developer, you’ll notice that the button Grant admin consent for <your Entra ID tenant name> is disabled, as shown in the following screenshot - you’re not authorized to use that function.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Grant admin consent disabled for application developer

That’s by design, because this request/approve workflow is designed with segregation of duties (SoD) in mind. Unless you have a privileged Entra ID user account on your own, you’ll need to ask your responsible Entra ID administrator to take over the remaining approval steps.

Eligible Entra ID administrators will need at least one of the following two directory roles to be able to grant admin consent:

  • Cloud Application Administrator (recommended)
  • Application Administrator

Assignment to the directory role will typically need to be activated using Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) at https://aka.ms/pim first, as illustrated next.

Use the Activate button next to Cloud Application Administrator to open a new form where you’ll need to provide at least a Reason for assignment activation. Finally, use the Activate button on that second form to apply your changes.

 

Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management: Activate Cloud Application Administrator Role

 

Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management: Finalize Activation of Cloud Application Administrator Role

Assignment to Cloud Application Administrator will be activated asynchronously. After a couple of seconds, a UI message should inform you that your set of active assignments has changed. Switch to the Active assignments tab in PIM and verify that the assignment is now in state Activated.

 

Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management: Verify Activation of Cloud Application Administrator Role

Granting Admin Consent for the Requested Application Permissions: Execution

Sign in to Microsoft Entra Admin Center at https://entra.microsoft.com using the privileged Entra ID user account who has an active assignment to directory role Cloud Application Administrator. Navigate to Entra ID > App registrations. Switch to the All applications tab and find idm-csv-client, keeping in mind that this display name is not unique. In case you have been experimenting and trying different things out, like I did, you may see more than one match when searching by display name. If in doubt, use the application (client) ID of idm-csv-client you noted down previously. This application (client) ID is unique, and you can use it to search just like the display name.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Find App Registration By Application (Client) ID

Click on the matching idm-csv-client entry, then navigate to its API permissions form. You’ll notice that the button Grant admin consent for <your Entra ID tenant name> is enabled, now that you are signed-in with a sufficiently privileged user. Use that button now and confirm the subsequent dialog with Yes.

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Grant admin consent > perform

Verify that the status of the requested application permission has changed from Not granted for … to Granted for ….

 

Microsoft Entra ID: Grant admin consent > verify

Wrap Up and Next Steps

Congratulations, you’ve completed all configuration required in Microsoft Entra ID. We can now use Entra ID as OAuth authorization server in an integration scenario for secure data migration from SAP IDM on premises into the public cloud. Your key takeaways from this blog are the following three important configuration properties, whose values you will need for the CSV client’s runtime:

  1. Application ID URI of idm-csv-server
  2. Application (client) ID of idm-csv-client
  3. Client secret of idm-csv-client

As you saw, the material discussed here was in many respects a cross-cutting topic at the intersection between integration and security concerns, and also between the SAP and Microsoft worlds. I hope readers interested in either or all of these fields found it worthwhile.

If you enjoyed the content presented here and wish to continue implementing the complete integration scenario end-to-end, I encourage you to head over to my companion tutorial on Codeberg. As mentioned in the introduction, the tutorial picks up from where this blog post leaves off and dives into SAP Integration Suite and SAP Cloud Connector in more detail. By the end of the tutorial, you will be able to fetch CSV exports from an on-premises SAP IDM via a secure, internet facing API that uses OAuth for authentication.

Have fun, happy hacking!

entry.title: SAP Principal Propagation via Web Dispatcher
entry.content:
In this Blog I will explain the detail concept of Principal Propagation and steps involved to configure the end to end setup.

The case is BTP application calling an on-premise ABAP system via Web Dispatcher with full identity propagation

And the Flow would be 

SAP BTP Application Destination → SAP Cloud Connector → SAP Web Dispatcher → On-Premise ABAP
Pre-Requisites

  • SCC already installed and running.
  • SCC connected to the correct BTP subaccount.
  • SCC administrator access.
  • SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS), SAML, X.509, or SPNEGO configured as the authentication provider.
  • Web Dispatcher installed and configured between client and backend systems.
  • Authenticated user identity must exist and be mapped consistently in all target SAP systems.
  • Trust relationship established between authentication provider and backend systems and Relevant certificates imported into trust stores (STRUST).



Let's understand the Concept

Conceptual Architecture

Important correction  Yes, importing the SCC system certificate trust into Web Dispatcher is mandatory in this topology. Web Dispatcher uses it to authenticate SCC as a trusted reverse proxy. Separately, the SCC CA signs the short-lived user certificate. These are two different certificates.

1 Trust architecture

Figure 1. Correct trust architecture, including SCC system certificate trust at Web Dispatcher

Diagram area

What happens

Why it is trusted

User → IdP → BTP

The user signs in. BTP gets a signed token containing the email.

SCC synchronizes and trusts the configured token issuer.

SCC Local CA

SCC converts the email identity into a short-lived X.509 certificate.

The SCC CA private key signs this temporary certificate.

SCC → Web Dispatcher

SCC presents the temporary certificate during HTTPS.

Web Dispatcher trusts the SCC principal-propagation CA chain.

Web Dispatcher → ABAP

Web Dispatcher opens a separate HTTPS/mTLS connection using its own client certificate.

ABAP trusts the exact Web Dispatcher subject and issuer as a reverse proxy.

SSL_CLIENT_CERT → CERTRULE

The validated public user certificate is forwarded and its CN email is mapped.

ABAP accepts the header only from the trusted proxy and maps it to SU01.

Runtime request flow

This sequence diagram shows the order of events for one request. Dashed vertical lines represent the participating systems. Each number happens after the previous number.

Step

Meaning

1

User authenticates and opens the BTP application.

2

The application calls a destination configured with PrincipalPropagation.

3

BTP Connectivity sends the request through the SCC tunnel.

4

SCC validates the token issuer and reads the mail attribute.

5

SCC creates a short-lived X.509 certificate and signs it with the SCC CA.

6

SCC presents that certificate to Web Dispatcher during the first TLS handshake.

7

Web Dispatcher validates issuer, signature, validity and certificate chain.

8

Web Dispatcher opens a second HTTPS/mTLS connection to ABAP with its own client certificate.

9

Web Dispatcher forwards the public user certificate in SSL_CLIENT_CERT.

10

ABAP verifies the trusted reverse proxy and CERTRULE maps CN email to SU01.

11

ABAP executes using the mapped user roles and returns the response.

TLS termination  The SCC-to-Web Dispatcher TLS session ends at Web Dispatcher. A new Web Dispatcher-to-ABAP TLS session begins. Therefore the user certificate is forwarded in a protected header, while Web Dispatcher authenticates the new session with its own certificate.

Principal propagation in one sentence

BTP user token → SCC reads email → SCC signs a temporary user certificate → Web Dispatcher validates and forwards it → ABAP trusts Web Dispatcher → CERTRULE maps the email to SU01 → PFCG controls authorization.

Beginner glossary

Term

Plain-language explanation

Certificate

An electronic identity card containing a subject, public key, issuer, serial number and validity dates.

Private key

The secret paired with a certificate. It creates signatures and proves possession. Never distribute it.

CA

Certificate Authority. A trusted signer that issues other certificates.

PKI

Public Key Infrastructure: people, policies, CAs and processes for issuing, renewing and revoking certificates.

PKI team

The security or infrastructure administrators who operate the corporate CA, such as Microsoft AD CS, DigiCert or Entrust.

CSR / PKCS#10

A Certificate Signing Request containing the requested subject and public key. It does not contain the private key.

PKCS#12

A password-protected .p12 or .pfx file that may contain a certificate, its private key and its chain.

DN

Distinguished Name, a comma-separated certificate identity such as CN, OU, O, L, ST and C.

CN

Common Name. Here, the CA CN names the CA and the temporary user certificate CN contains email.

SAN

Subject Alternative Name. The DNS name used for modern HTTPS hostname verification.

PSE

SAP Personal Security Environment containing a certificate, private key and trusted public CA certificates.

TLS / mTLS

TLS encrypts HTTPS. mTLS also authenticates the client with a client certificate.

Listener

A protocol and TCP port where Web Dispatcher waits for inbound connections.

SSL_CLIENT_CERT

The protected HTTP header carrying the public user certificate from trusted Web Dispatcher to ABAP.

Certificate terms:

DN field

Meaning

Example

CN

Common Name

SCC Principal Propagation CA PRD

OU

Organizational Unit

SAP Security

O

Organization

Contoso India Private Limited

L

City

Thane

ST

State

Maharashtra

C

Two-letter country code

IN

Exact implementation steps

Step 1. Configure the SCC system certificate

  1. SCC Administration → Configuration → On Premise → System Certificate.
  2. Generate a CSR and then import a company-signed system certificate.
  3. Use a subject such as CN=scc-dev.sap.contoso.net, OU=SAP Cloud Connector, O=contoso Private Limited, C=IN.
  4. Download the SCC system certificate in DER format.
  5. Also obtain the public certificate of its issuing CA and any intermediate CA certificates.
  6. Copy the exact SCC system certificate Subject and Issuer. You need both in Web Dispatcher profile parameters.

What to export  If the SCC system certificate is CA-signed, import its issuing CA chain into WD trust. If it is self-signed, import the SCC system certificate itself.

 

Step 2. Configure the SCC principal-propagation CA

  1. SCC Administration → Configuration → On Premise → CA Certificate.
  2. For production, choose Generate Certificate Signing Request.
  3. Use CN=SAP-Cloud-Connector-RootCA-Dev, OU=SAP, O=Contoso Private Limited, C=IN.
  4. Ask the PKI team to issue it as a subordinate CA with CA=TRUE and keyCertSign.
  5. Import the signed CA response and complete chain into SCC.
  6. Verify the CA private key is present and the certificate is valid.
  7. Download the SCC CA public certificate in DER format for backend certificate-chain validation and operational records.

Do not confuse these  The system certificate authenticates SCC as a machine. The CA certificate signs short-lived user certificates. Do not use the BTP Secure Login Service for SAP GUI as this CA.

We are using Local CA here meaning self-signed certificate, since system certificate is CA signed.

Step 3. Configure the SCC user certificate subject

  1. SCC → Configuration → On Premise → Principal Propagation → Edit.
  2. Set the subject pattern to the email value shown below.
  3. Save.
  4. Create a sample certificate for a real-format test email.
  5. Download the sample certificate as DER for CERTRULE.

CN=${email}, OU=SAP CC, O=Contoso Private Limited, C=IN

Step 4. Make Web Dispatcher trust the SCC system certificate

  1. Open https://<wd-host>:<admin-port>/sap/wdisp/admin.
  2. Navigate to SSL and Trust Configuration → PSE Management.
  3. Select SAPSSLS.pse. This is the Web Dispatcher server PSE for inbound HTTPS.
  4. Under Trusted Certificates, choose Import Certificate. 
  5. If SCC system certificate is CA-signed, import the issuing root/intermediate CA certificates. If self-signed, import the SCC system certificate itself.
  6. Save and confirm that imported certificate appears in Trusted Certificates.
  7. Issuer certificate was already there but keep in mind if it’s not there then we need to upload that also.
  8. Copy the exact Subject and Issuer of the SCC system certificate from SCC.
  9. Add below Web Dispatcher profile parameter. (Parameters à edit parameters
  10. Restart or reconfigure Web Dispatcher using your controlled change procedure.

    icm/trusted_reverse_proxy_0 = SUBJECT="<Subject SCC System Certificate", ISSUER="Issuer of System cert"

    icm/trusted_reverse_proxy_1 = SUBJECT="<Subject SCC System Certificate", ISSUER="Issuer of System cert"

 

 

Verify parameters in Instance profile (Its best if we restart the web dispatcher after setting parameters) 

Exact result  Web Dispatcher now authenticates SCC using the SCC system certificate and is allowed to accept a forwarded user certificate from that SCC connection.

Step 5. Configure the Web Dispatcher inbound HTTPS listener and forwarding

  1. Ensure the SCC-facing listener uses HTTPS and the WD server certificate SAN contains the exact SCC internal host name.
  2. Use a dedicated port such as 44380 where possible.
  3. Set VCLIENT=1 on the listener, or verify_client=1 globally.
  4. Enable certificate forwarding with forward_ccert_as_header=true.
  5. Run Web Dispatcher configuration validation and restart/reconfigure.
  6. Add below parameters for inbound listener and forwarding

                     icm/server_port_0 = PROT=HTTPS,PORT=44380,VCLIENT=1

                      icm/HTTPS/verify_client = 1

                      icm/HTTPS/forward_ccert_as_header = true

  • An HTTPS listener (icm/server_port_0) is the Web Dispatcher port accepting encrypted connections. Its server certificate proves to SCC that the correct Web Dispatcher host was reached.
  • VCLIENT and verify_client control the user client-certificate request and validation behavior. Confirm exact values for your kernel release.
  • forward_ccert_as_header places the validated certificate into the SAP certificate-forwarding header.

Step 6. Configure Web Dispatcher outbound HTTPS to ABAP

  1. In WD PSE Management, identify SAPSSLC.pse used for outbound HTTPS.
  2. Generate a WD backend client certificate with TLS Web Client Authentication.
  3. Use subject CN=wd-dev.sap.contoso.net, OU=SAP Web Dispatcher Backend Client, O=Contoso Private Limited, C=IN.
  4. Import the ABAP HTTPS server issuing CA chain into SAPSSLC.pse so that WD trusts ABAP.
  5. Copy the exact WD backend client certificate Subject and Issuer for ABAP trusted_reverse_proxy configuration.
  6. Required outcome  The WD-to-ABAP hop must be HTTPS/mTLS. WD presents its own client certificate; it forwards the user certificate separately in SSL_CLIENT_CERT.

     

     

     Ensure ABAP HTTPS server issuing CA chain into SAPSSLC.pse so that WD trusts ABAP

     

    Step 7. Make ABAP trust Web Dispatcher

    1. ABAP transaction STRUST → SSL Server Standard → Change.
    2. Import the issuing CA of the WD backend client certificate. If it is self-signed, import the WD client certificate itself.
    3. Choose Add to Certificate List and Save.
    4. Transaction RZ10 → DEFAULT profile → Extended Maintenance.
    5. Add the ABAP trusted_reverse_proxy parameter below with the WD client certificate Subject and Issuer.
    6. Ensure the HTTPS listener has VCLIENT=1 or icm/HTTPS/verify_client=1.
    7. Ensure login/certificate_mapping_rulebased=1.
    8. Save and activate the profile.
    9. Restart the system, If the Landscape is RISE then raise an SR to SAP.

      icm/trusted_reverse_proxy_0 = SUBJECT="<WD Subject", ISSUER = “<WD Issuer>”
      icm/HTTPS/verify_client = 1

      login/certificate_mapping_rulebased = 1

    Step 9. Configure CERTRULE mapping

    1. Open CERTRULE TCODE in ABAP --> Configuration --> Upload Certificate
    2. Import the SCC sample user certificate from step 3.

  • Create a rule restricted to the SCC principal-propagation CA issuer.
  • Certificate attribute = CN.
  • Login As = E-Mail.
  • Save.

Step 10. Configure Web Dispatcher hostname in SCC

  1. SCC → connected subaccount → Cloud To On-Premise → Access Control → Add.
  2. Back-end Type = ABAP System.
  3. Protocol = HTTPS.
  4. Internal Host = wd-dev.sap.contoso.net.
  5. Internal Port = 44380.
  6. Virtual Host = abap-dev-pp.sap.contoso.net.
  7. Virtual Port = 443.
  8. Enable Allow Principal Propagation.
  9. Principal Type = X.509 Certificate.
  10. Add only required resources, for example /sap/opu/odata/<namespace>/<service>/.

Step 11. Configure the BTP destination

Name=ABAP_DEV_PP
Type=HTTP
URL=http://<virtual host>
ProxyType=OnPremise
Authentication=PrincipalPropagation
CloudConnectorLocationId=<ONLY_IF_CONFIGURED_IN_SCC>

Save the destination.
Hit check connection on Destination, it should work now. Do the testing with end users as well.

Step 12. Test in this order

Test

Pass condition

If it fails

1. SCC mapping Check Availability

HTTPS reachable; server name valid; mTLS details show SCC system certificate.

SCC logs, DNS, firewall, WD server certificate SAN, SAPSSLS trust.

2. WD inbound

dev_webdisp shows SCC system certificate accepted and trusted proxy matched.

WD SAPSSLS.pse, verify_client, WD trusted_reverse_proxy.

3. User certificate at WD

Forwarded short-lived certificate is present; CN contains email.

SCC subject template, SCC CA, principal type.

4. WD to ABAP

ABAP validates WD client certificate.

SAPSSLC.pse, ABAP SSL Server Standard, backend TLS.

5. Header acceptance

ABAP accepts SSL_CLIENT_CERT only from WD.

ABAP trusted_reverse_proxy subject/issuer.

6. CERTRULE

One email maps to one SU01 user.

CERTRULE issuer/CN rule and SU01 email.

7. Authorization

Business service succeeds under mapped user.

SICF, SU53, STAUTHTRACE, /IWFND/ERROR_LOG.

Thus ends the configuration of PP. Do let me know if you have any questions in comment section.

Thank You !

Best Regards,

Prashant

entry.title: How to Simulate a SAP BTP Request to an On-Premise S/4HANA System Using Postman
entry.content:
How to Simulate a SAP BTP Request to an On-Premise S/4HANA System Using Postman

I recently ran into an issue while trying to consume data from the standard APIs exposed by an on-premise S/4HANA system through the CAP backend of a Fiori application deployed on SAP BTP and exposed via SAP Build Work Zone. The requests were failing at the Cloud Connector level, but I couldn’t find any error logs or relevant traces, either in SAP Cloud Connector or on the S/4HANA side.

To narrow down the root cause, I decided to test the API call directly from Postman, simulating a request originating from BTP so that the traffic would go through the SAP Cloud Connector. This allowed me to isolate the connectivity layer and determine whether the issue was related to the Cloud Connector configuration, the BTP configuration, the S/4HANA backend, or the CAP application itself.

I couldn’t find any end-to-end blog post or tutorial covering this specific scenario. That’s why I decided to share my experience here, along with the key steps and configuration required to get it working. The Postman collection used in the tutorial can be found on GitHub.

TL;DR

This approach did not directly identify the root cause of the error in Postman, but since the Postman request was successful, it allowed both the SAP S/4HANA system and the SAP Cloud Connector configuration to be ruled out as potential causes.

I therefore focused my investigation on the BTP side. I discovered that the destination I expected to be used at the subaccount level correctly configured and pointing to the appropriate virtual host URL of the on-premise system was actually being overridden by another destination with the same name, defined at the Cloud Foundry space level in the Destination service instance. This space-level destination contained an incorrect URL, which explained why the requests originating from the CAP application were failing.

Understanding SAP Cloud Connector

Communication between SAP S/4HANA and the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) is established through a secure tunnel provided by the SAP Cloud Connector. The Cloud Connector enables secure connectivity between on-premise systems and SAP BTP without exposing internal servers directly to the Internet.

The connection is initiated from the on-premise network, with the SAP Cloud Connector establishing an outbound TLS connection to SAP BTP. BTP therefore does not need to initiate an inbound connection to the on-premise network, eliminating the need to open inbound ports in the corporate firewall.

The SAP Cloud Connector then maps a virtual host (Virtual Host) to the corresponding internal host (Internal Host) of the SAP S/4HANA system. Applications running on SAP BTP use the virtual host when making requests to the on-premise system. The Cloud Connector transparently routes these requests to the mapped internal host through the established secure tunnel.

Understanding SAP Connectivity Service

On the SAP BTP side, the Connectivity service is responsible for managing communication with remote systems. It provides a mechanism to define objects called Destinations, which centralize the connection parameters required by applications to access target systems, such as the URL, authentication settings, proxy configuration, and other connectivity-related properties.

The Connectivity service also provides an internal HTTP proxy that is accessible only from SAP BTP runtime environments. This proxy acts as the communication layer between applications running on BTP and on-premise systems, routing requests through the SAP Cloud Connector.

This architecture keeps the connectivity endpoint isolated from the public Internet. As a result, external clients such as Postman or locally running applications cannot directly access this internal proxy endpoint. Only applications running within the appropriate SAP BTP runtime environment can use it to reach the on-premise system through the established Cloud Connector tunnel.

Request Flow

To reproduce, using Postman, the communication flow of a request sent by the CAP backend of a SAP Fiori application deployed on SAP BTP to an on-premise SAP S/4HANA system, we need to replicate the same communication path and connectivity components involved in the original request.

Step 1: Obtain an OAuth Access Token for SAP BTP Connectivity

To access the SAP BTP network proxy from outside the BTP runtime environment, Postman must first obtain an access token. This is done by sending a POST request from Postman to the UAA authentication endpoint exposed by the SAP BTP Connectivity service.

First, create an instance of the Connectivity service and generate a dedicated Service Key for this test scenario. 

The Service Key contains the credentials and endpoint information required to authenticate with the Connectivity service and obtain the OAuth access token. 

For the token request, the base authentication URL is provided in the url property of the Service Key. To obtain the OAuth access token, append the /oauth/token suffix to this URL.

The Authorization header of the token request contains the application credentials used to authenticate against SAP BTP. For this request, I use Basic Authentication, with the clientid and clientsecret values from the Service Key as the username and password, respectively. 

The request body contains the grant_type parameter set to password, along with the username and password of a user account from the BTP subaccount. This allows me to obtain an OAuth access token by authenticating on behalf of that user account. The resulting token can then be used to authenticate subsequent requests through the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy.

Send the request to obtain the JWT access token. This token acts as a credential that allows Postman to authenticate with the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy and demonstrate that it is an authorized client. Without a valid access token, the BTP Connectivity proxy will reject the request at the next step with a 407 Proxy Authentication Required response.

Step 2: Establish the SSH Network Tunnel

Before sending the request to the S/4HANA system, we need to address a second infrastructure-level challenge: the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy is exposed through a private IP address that is not directly reachable from the public Internet, where Postman is running.

To overcome this limitation, we establish an SSH tunnel (port forwarding) to a Cloud Foundry application that has access to the Connectivity service. This tunnel acts as a technical bridge, forwarding traffic from our local port (localhost:20003) directly to the private IP address and port of the BTP Connectivity proxy (X.X.X.X:20003). This allows Postman to effectively reach the BTP Connectivity proxy as if the request were originating from within the BTP environment.

Open a terminal and log in to the Cloud Foundry environment using cf api and cf login. Enable SSH access for the application and the Cloud Foundry space by running the following commands:

cf enable-ssh <APP_NAME>
cf allow-space-ssh <SPACE_NAME>
cf restage <APP_NAME>

Once SSH access has been enabled for both the application and the Cloud Foundry space, open the SSH tunnel using the following command:

ssh <app-name> -N -T -L <onpremise_proxy_http_port>:<onpremise_proxy_host>:<forwarded_local_port>

In my case, I reused local port 20003, as it was not already in use on my machine.

Step 3: Configure the Proxy and Send the Business Request to SAP S/4HANA

Once the network tunnel and access token are in place, we can configure the final request in Postman to retrieve business data from the SAP S/4HANA API_BUSINESS_PARTNER API. The request URL uses the Virtual Host and Virtual Port exposed and configured in the SAP Cloud Connector.

In Postman’s global settings, configure a Custom Proxy pointing to localhost:20003, which is the local entry point of our SSH tunnel. This configuration routes the request through the SSH tunnel to the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy, allowing Postman to leverage the BTP connectivity path to reach the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system.

In the Proxy Server configuration, enter the following values:

  • Protocol: http
  • Host: localhost
  • Port: <forwarded_local_port>

In Postman, create a new GET request to retrieve data from the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system. The request URL is composed of the following elements:

  • The Virtual Host of the SAP S/4HANA system exposed through the SAP Cloud Connector.
  • The Business Partner OData service URI: /sap/opu/odata/SAP/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner
  • The query parameters used to specify the SAP client and limit the number of Business Partners returned: ?sap-client=<client>&$top=10. In this example, $top=10 limits the response to the first 10 Business Partners.

In the Authorization tab, configure Basic Auth and provide the SAP S/4HANA system credentials (Username / Password) required to access the API.

The SAP BTP Connectivity proxy and the SAP Cloud Connector essentially act as a secure communication layer for routing the request. Once the request reaches the SAP S/4HANA system, it still needs to be authenticated and authorized by the SAP Gateway.

The Basic Authentication credentials provided in the request are therefore used by SAP S/4HANA to authenticate the caller and determine whether the user has the required authorizations to access or modify the requested business data.

To authenticate the request against the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy, we manually add the Proxy-Authorization header in Postman’s Headers tab. There is a technical detail worth mentioning here: Postman handles the Proxy-Authorization header, but this particular scenario requires a non-standard Basic Authentication format where the username is the JWT access token and the password is empty. Therefore, we need to Base64-encode the following string: "<token_jwt>:". The trailing colon (:) is important because it separates the username from the empty password. The resulting value is then sent in the following format:

Proxy-Authorization: Basic <Base64_encoded_value>

This allows the BTP Connectivity proxy to extract the JWT from the Basic Authentication credentials and validate the request before forwarding it through the Connectivity path. To automate this step, I use an After Response script in the first request to retrieve the token_jwt and encode it in Base64. This allows the Proxy-Authorization header to be generated dynamically from the access token  : 

const jsonData = pm.response.json();
pm.test("Status code is 200", function () {
    pm.response.to.have.status(200);
});

pm.test("Access token is present", function () {
    pm.expect(jsonData.access_token).to.be.a('string');
    pm.collectionVariables.set("access_token", jsonData.access_token);
});

const token = pm.collectionVariables.get("access_token");
const rawString = token + ":";
const base64Encoded = "Basic " + btoa(rawString);
pm.collectionVariables.set("base64EncodedToken", base64Encoded);

If you use a Location ID to identify your SAP Cloud Connector instance, you must also include it in the request headers using the SAP-Connectivity-SCC-Location_ID header.

Request Flow

When clicking Send in Postman, the request follows the complete connectivity path:

  1. Postman sends the request through the local SSH tunnel.
  2. The request reaches the Cloud Foundry application running on SAP BTP.
  3. The request is authenticated by the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy using the JWT access token.
  4. The Connectivity proxy routes the request through the SAP Cloud Connector tunnel.
  5. The request reaches the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system.
  6. SAP S/4HANA authenticates the request using the configured Basic Authentication credentials and executes the requested operation.

This reproduces, from Postman, the same connectivity path used by the CAP backend of the Fiori application to communicate with the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system.

Don’t forget to close the SSH tunnel and disable SSH access on the Cloud Foundry application and space once testing is complete.

Conclusion

Using Postman as a troubleshooting tool allowed me to isolate the issue and rule out both the SAP S/4HANA system and the SAP Cloud Connector configuration as potential root causes. Since the request successfully reached S/4HANA and returned the expected data, I was able to focus my investigation on the SAP BTP side.

I discovered that the destination configured at the subaccount level was correctly pointing to the Virtual Host of the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system. However, a destination with the same name was also defined at the Cloud Foundry space level through the Destination service instance. This second destination contained an incorrect URL. When destinations with the same name exist both at the subaccount level and in a Destination service instance bound to the application, the instance-level destination takes precedence during destination resolution. As a result, the application was using the incorrect Virtual Host URL from the Destination service instance instead of the correctly configured subaccount-level destination. This also explained why no corresponding requests or errors were visible on the SAP Cloud Connector side: the request was never reaching the Cloud Connector in the first place.

Although this is a fairly specific troubleshooting scenario, I hope this walkthrough can help you diagnose similar connectivity issues between SAP BTP and on-premise SAP S/4HANA systems. If you know of any other approaches, simpler troubleshooting techniques, or alternative ways to achieve the same result, feel free to share them in the comments. I’d be happy to hear about your experience and learn from other approaches.

Thanks for reading!

entry.title: Connecting SAP to Power BI Through SAP BTP: Architecture Decisions and Lessons Learned
entry.content:
I work with the team behind Power BI Connector for SAP by Metrica Software. This post shares the architectural decisions and practical lessons that emerged while developing an SAP BTP-based connection between SAP and Power BI.

It is not a configuration guide. My goal is to discuss the problems that appear after the first successful connection and the design choices we made to address them.

The Problem Beyond the First Power BI SAP Connection

A basic SAP-to-Power BI scenario can appear straightforward:

  1. Make an SAP OData service available.
  2. Add its URL to Power BI.
  3. Authenticate.
  4. Load the required entities.

This can be enough for an isolated report. The architecture becomes more difficult when several Power BI reports require different combinations of SAP data.

One report may need sales orders, order items, customers, and products. Another may use some of the same entities but require different fields or filters. Separate teams may also need access to the same data without sharing credentials or receiving broader SAP access than their work requires.

At that point, several questions arise:

  • Where should the reporting scope be defined?
  • Who decides which SAP services and fields can be used?
  • How can the same configuration be reused?
  • How can access be revoked for one Power BI user?
  • How do we determine whether a failed refresh reached the SAP integration layer?
  • Who changed the configuration used by a report?

These questions influenced the architecture more than the initial OData connection itself.

Why We Used SAP BTP as the Access Layer

We placed the integration layer in SAP BTP rather than creating a separate externally managed extraction environment.

For SAP S/4HANA On-Premise and Private Cloud, the connection uses SAP Cloud Connector and an SAP BTP destination. This allows the SAP administrators to control which backend system and resources are reachable from BTP.

For SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud, the connection follows the standard Communication Arrangement model. A communication user and the corresponding communication scenario provide access to the required services without SAP Cloud Connector.

The same OData-based model can be applied to SAP ECC and SAP BW when the necessary services are available.

This design keeps an important responsibility with the SAP team. The integration layer cannot read arbitrary SAP data. Its maximum access is determined by the configured destination, available OData services, and the authorizations assigned to the relevant technical or communication user.

Separate SAP Access from the Reporting Scope

One of our main design decisions was to separate backend access from the data scope of an individual Power BI report.

SAP roles and authorizations define what the integration is permitted to read. However, a report rarely needs everything that the technical user can access.

For this reason, we introduced a reporting data source as a separate configuration. It defines:

  • Which SAP OData services are used
  • Which entities are exposed
  • Which fields are included
  • Which filters are applied
  • Which users can consume the result

For example, the technical user may have access to a sales order service, but a regional Power BI model may require only selected fields and records for specific company codes.

Applying that scope before returning data to Power BI has two benefits. Less unnecessary data is transferred, and the configuration clearly documents what the report is expected to receive.

We also found that previewing the selected data and entity relationships before connecting Power BI was important. It is easier to identify an incorrect entity, missing field, or unsuitable filter before the configuration becomes a dependency for a semantic model.

Make the SAP Configuration Reusable

Another lesson was that SAP connectivity and report development have different lifecycles.

A PBIX file may be copied, replaced, or divided into several reports. The approved SAP data scope should not need to be reconstructed every time this happens.

We therefore treated each reporting source as a reusable configuration with its own stable OData endpoint. Multiple Power BI reports can use the same endpoint when they require the same SAP scope.

This also reduces inconsistency. If different report authors independently select services, fields, and filters, reports that appear to use the same SAP data may produce different results. A shared source gives them a common starting point.

Reuse does not mean that every report must use one central configuration. When a user needs a different scope, the existing source can be cloned and adjusted without changing the configuration used by other reports.

Use Individual Credentials for Power BI Connections

Shared technical credentials are convenient initially, but they make user-level access difficult to trace or revoke.

We chose to authenticate Power BI connections with the connector username and a personal access token through HTTP Basic authentication. The token takes the place of the password.

Each token belongs to an individual connector user and can be revoked independently. Tokens can also have an expiry policy and descriptive labels, such as “Power BI Desktop” or “Power BI Service refresh.”

This distinction becomes particularly useful when a data source is shared. The recipient uses the same OData endpoint but authenticates with their own token. The owner’s credential is never passed to the recipient.

The shared configuration remains read-only. A recipient can inspect it, preview the data, use it in Power BI, or clone it into an independently owned configuration. The recipient cannot modify, delete, re-share, or transfer the original source.

If access is removed, the recipient’s token can no longer use that endpoint. This provides more precise control than distributing one credential across several reports and users.

Audit More Than Successful Refreshes

A connection is not fully manageable if the only available signal is whether the Power BI report contains recent data.

We found that three types of history were needed.

Data Source History

Changes to a reporting source should be recorded, including creation, updates, cloning, deletion, and ownership transfer.

For updates, a before-and-after view is particularly useful. It shows whether someone added or removed an SAP service, entity, field, or filter expression. This helps explain why a report’s structure or results changed.

Access Token History

The token lifecycle should also be traceable. Recording issuance, expiration, and revocation helps administrators determine whether authentication changes are responsible for a failed refresh.

Export History

Every OData read against a reporting endpoint should create a record containing the time, data source, token owner, token label, response status, and request duration.

This information helps answer practical operational questions:

  • Did the scheduled Power BI refresh reach the endpoint?
  • Did it fail with 401 because the token expired?
  • Did it return 403 because the user lost access to the source?
  • Which reporting source is being requested most frequently?
  • How long did the request, including the SAP backend call, take?

We made this history read-only so that it functions as an audit trail rather than another editable data set.

What This Architecture Does Not Solve

This architecture provides a controlled route from SAP OData services to Power BI, but it does not remove the need for data modelling.

The connection uses Power BI Import mode. Relationships, calculated columns, measures, business definitions, and report logic still need to be created in the Power BI semantic model.

It also depends on the quality and availability of the SAP OData services. If the required business data is not exposed through a suitable service, the access layer cannot create it. Changes to an existing service can affect the reporting sources and Power BI models that depend on it.

Source-side filters also need to be designed carefully. Restricting records can reduce data transfer and keep the scope appropriate, but an overly narrow filter may prevent Power BI from performing the analysis required later.

Finally, audit history helps locate a problem, but it does not automatically correct an expired token, an authorization change, or an SAP service error. Those events still require action from the relevant Power BI, BTP, or SAP administrator.

Lessons Learned

The most important lesson was that connecting SAP to Power BI should be treated as an operating model, not only as a working endpoint.

The SAP team should define the maximum backend access. Reporting configurations should narrow that access for specific analytical purposes. Power BI users should connect with individual credentials. Frequently used SAP scopes should be reusable, and changes and requests should remain traceable after reports enter production.

This separation gives each team a clearer responsibility:

  • SAP administrators control services and business authorizations.
  • BTP administrators control backend connectivity.
  • Data source owners prepare and maintain the reporting scope.
  • Power BI developers build semantic models and reports from that approved scope.

There is no single architecture that fits every SAP and Power BI environment. For us, SAP BTP, OData services, reusable reporting sources, individual tokens, and a detailed audit history formed a practical foundation.

I would be interested to hear how other teams divide these responsibilities and monitor SAP-backed Power BI refreshes in their own environments.

entry.title: Principal Propagation for MCP Servers - SAP Integration Suite to SAP S/4HANA On-Premise
entry.content:
Introduction

MCP Servers can now be built and deployed on SAP Integration Suite, turning existing OData services and other SAP APIs into tools that MCP-capable clients can discover and invoke. For guidance on what to expose as MCP tools and how to think about the design, see my earlier post: Building MCP Servers with SAP Integration Suite — what to design, not just how.

Once your MCP Server is running, the next question is inevitable: how does the identity of the calling user reach the backend? For on-premise (or private cloud) SAP systems reachable via SAP Cloud Connector, the answer is Principal Propagation — the same mechanism used by every other BTP-to-on-premise integration scenario.

This post covers the end-to-end setup for the generic case: any MCP client (MCP Inspector, Joule Work Desktop, etc.) authenticating against SAP Default or IAS IdP, calling an MCP Server artifact on SAP Integration Suite, which then reaches S/4HANA on-premise through Cloud Connector as the real calling user.

Note: A parallel guide already exists for the Copilot Studio and Microsoft Entra ID — see SAP × Microsoft Copilot Studio — MCP Gateway guides series, Guide 04 for that variant, which also contains a thorough ABAP-side walkthrough.

The working example used throughout this post is API_BUSINESS_PARTNER on S/4HANA on-premise; the same setup applies identically to S/4HANA private cloud.

Scope: This post covers on-premise and private cloud ABAP systems reachable via Cloud Connector. For S/4HANA Public Cloud, the mechanism is different — the destination uses OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion instead of PrincipalPropagation, and no Cloud Connector is involved. That scenario is covered in detail by blogpost: MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose S/4HANA Public Cloud API via OAuth2SAMLBearer.

Architecture

At the highest level, four hops carry user identity from an MCP client all the way to a real SAP user in S/4HANA — JWT on the BTP side, X.509 on the Cloud Connector side:

Prerequisites

BTP Subaccount

  • A business-user OIDC IdP is active: either SAP Default (sap.default, present out of the box) or a customer IAS tenant configured as a business-user OIDC IdP under Security → Trust Configuration.
  • The calling user has the API.invoke role assigned — either directly via a role collection, or as part of a custom one. This is the built-in Integration Suite role that gates all API and MCP Server calls from IdP users. See Creating a Custom Role Collection for Fine-Grained Access Control for how to set this up.

Cloud Connector

For the complete certificate generation walkthrough — System Certificate, CA Certificate, and User/Sample Certificate — follow Navin Krishnan's blog, which covers each step in detail.

Validate that:

  • System Certificate — used for the CC-to-S/4 mTLS handshake; downloaded and imported later into S/4's STRUST.
  • CA Certificate — the CA that signs every short-lived user certificate CPI mints per request.
  • User (Sample) Certificate — generated with a Subject Pattern such as ${mail} or ${user_uuid}; used to define the mapping rule in CERTRULE on the backend.
  • System mapping for the S/4 backend, with Principal Type = X.509 Certificate (General Usage).
  • Principal Propagation is synced from the subaccount: Cloud to On-Premises → Principal Propagation → Synchronize. The Trust Configuration table must show at least two IDP entries — if it shows (0), PP will silently fail inside CPI before any request reaches the tunnel.

S/4HANA (on-premise / private cloud)

Validate that:

  • STRUST: the CC System Certificate is imported into the SSL Server Standard PSE.
  • CERTRULE: the sample user certificate is imported and a rule mapping the certificate attribute (e.g. E-Mail) to SU01 users is defined.
  • RZ10:
    • icm/trusted_reverse_proxy_0 = SUBJECT="CN=<system-cert-CN>", ISSUER="CN=<CA-CN>"
    • login/certificate_mapping_rulebased = 1
  • SMICM: hard-restart ICM only if you changed the RZ10 profile parameters above.

SAP Integration Suite — Destination

Create a destination on the subaccount with:

Property Value

TypeHTTP
URLhttp://<virtual-host>:<virtual-port>
Proxy TypeOnPremise
AuthenticationPrincipalPropagation
Location ID<cc-location-id> (if non-default)
sap-client (additional property)<client number>

The virtual host and port must match the CC system mapping exactly. Reference this destination from the HTTP receiver in your MCP Server artifact.

Building and Registering the MCP Server

Deploy the MCP Server

SAP Integration Suite lets you create an MCP Server directly from an OpenAPI specification. The steps below use API_BUSINESS_PARTNER API as the example.

1. Download the OpenAPI specification

Download the OpenAPI specification file for your target API from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub:

  • Business Partner

2. Create and configure the MCP Server artifact

In Integration Suite, go to Design → Integrations and APIs and create a new artifact. Choose MCP Server as the artifact type, then set the source type to HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification and fill in the following:

Property Value

File NameThe OpenAPI .json file downloaded above
SourceDestination
DestinationThe BTP destination created in the Prerequisites section
Relative URLThe OData service path, e.g. /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER
MCP PathAny path ending with /mcp, e.g. /businesspartner/mcp

3. Select tools to expose

From the parsed spec, select the operations you want to expose as MCP tools. A maximum of 30 tools can be included per MCP Server artifact.

4. Configure Authentication

Leave the Authentication policy settings as-is — the default configuration handles the inbound JWT validation automatically.

5. Configure Authorization

Under Authorization, keep the default API.invoke role. Ensure this role is assigned to the calling user via a role collection (see Prerequisites).

6. Deploy

Before deploying, you can optionally add Security or Traffic Management policies to the MCP Server artifact — for example, rate limiting or IP allowlisting. These are applied in the Policies tab if required.

Once you ready, deploy the MCP Server. Note the MCP URL of the deployed artifact.

Publish as an API Product in Developer Hub

Once deployed, the MCP Server needs to be published as a product in Developer Hub so clients can discover it and obtain OAuth credentials.

  1. Open Developer Hub → Admin Center → Content.

  2. Select your Business System → Integration Suite.

  3. Select the MCP Server artifact you've deployed and choose Create Product.

  4. Once your request to publish a product is successfully processed, you will find it in the list of available products.

Create a Subscription for your MCP Client

In Developer Hub, navigate to the product and open Create New Subscription for Agent. Fill in a Name and, optionally, a Short Text and Description. The field that matters most is Callback URL:

The Callback URL is the OAuth redirect_uri the platform sends the authorization code back to after the user logs in. It must match exactly what your MCP client expects.

For example:

  • For MCP Inspector: http://localhost:6274/oauth/callback
  • For Joule Work Desktop: http://localhost:18766/mcp-callback (validate that JWD runs on port 18766)

Leave Take me to this new subscription now checked and click Create. Developer Hub opens the subscription details page. Wait until the Credentials are generated.

You now have everything the client needs:

  • The MCP Server endpoint URL (from the deployed artifact)
  • The OAuth Client ID and Secret (Key and Secret from the subscription credentials)

Testing

MCP Inspector

MCP Inspector is the open-source reference client for MCP, useful for initial validation because it exposes every request, response, and token in plain view.

MCP Inspector can be installed and run locally via:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector

In the Inspector UI:

  1. Click Add Servers → Add manually.
  2. Set Transport to streamable-http and URL to your deployed MCP Server endpoint. Click Add.
  3. Click Settings for the newly added server. Under OAuth Settings set:
    • Client ID as Key from the Developer Hub subscription
    • Client Secret as Secret from the Developer Hub subscription
  4. Toggle Connect. Inspector opens a browser tab, the IdP login screen appears, and after successful authentication the authorization code is exchanged for a JWT. Inspector attaches this token to every subsequent MCP request via the X-Mcp-Remote-Auth header.
  5. Navigate to the Tools tab and invoke your MCP tool.

▶ Watch the MCP Inspector demo

Joule Work Desktop

Joule Work Desktop (JWD) is the SAP-native MCP-capable client. Setup is lighter because token acquisition and refresh are handled natively.

  1. In JWD, add a new MCP Server connector.
  2. Enter the MCP Server endpoint URL and the Client ID / Secret from the Developer Hub subscription.
  3. When prompted, sign in via the IdP. JWD handles the authorization-code flow, stores the tokens, and refreshes them automatically.
  4. Open a new Conversation, attach your MCP Connector to the conversation and ask e.g. to list 5 business partners.

▶ Watch the Joule Work Desktop demo

Verify Principal Propagation

Open Cloud Connector → Monitor → Most Recent Requests. Each MCP tool call should appear as a row, with the propagated user visible in the request details.

References

  • Building MCP Servers with SAP Integration Suite — what to design, not just how
  • Principal propagation setup with SAP S/4HANA on-premise system and SAP Business Technology Platform
  • SAP × Microsoft Copilot Studio MCP Gateway series, Guide 04
  • SAP Help — Configuring Principal Propagation
  • SAP Reference Architecture — MCP Gateway
  • MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose S/4HANA Public Cloud API via OAuth2SAMLBearer

entry.title: SAP BTP Work Zone - Authentication and Authorization, with On prem system
entry.content:
Recently I was working on deploying apps from SAP BTP and an on-premise SAP S/4HANA system to SAP Build Work Zone. The most important question from stakeholders was: how does access actually work when the app itself lives in S/4HANA? This post answers that question first with a simple example, and then walks through the configuration I used to make it work.

To make it easy to understand, imagine you run an enterprise called Central Inc. You want every employee to have one single launchpad to access apps from different systems: S/4HANA (Finance), SuccessFactors (HR) and Ariba (Procurement). That central launchpad is SAP Build Work Zone.

The Scene: Two Keys Needed for Every User

Our user, Maria, works in Procurement. To do her job, she needs access to the Create Purchase Order app.

This app lives inside the S/4HANA system, but we want her to launch it from Work Zone. This requires two distinct keys working together.

Key 1: The UI Key (Federated BTP Role Collection)

Work Zone uses content federation. It imports the S/4HANA UI content (business roles, spaces, pages and tiles) into Work Zone, so nothing has to be rebuilt manually in the cloud.

For every federated business role, a BTP role collection is generated automatically, named after the content provider ID and the backend role, e.g. ~s4h_SAP_BR_PURCHASER.

What this key does: When Maria logs in to Work Zone, her identity (via SAP Cloud Identity Services / Microsoft Entra ID) is mapped to this role collection. This lets her see and click the Purchase Order tile on her homepage. This key only gets her into the lobby of the building.

Key 2: The Data Key (Backend PFCG Role)

Maria clicks the tile. The app is now running and needs to read and write live data in S/4HANA.

Principal propagation through the SAP Cloud Connector securely passes Maria's identity down to S/4HANA. S/4HANA maps it to her local user (SU01) and checks: does Maria have the PFCG role SAP_BR_PURCHASER (and its authorizations) in this system?

What this key does: If the role is assigned, she is authorized to work with the specific business data. This key opens the locked office door and gives access to the actual files.

Configuration Walkthrough

Below are the steps I followed to set this up end to end. Names such as s4h and S4H_RT are examples; use your own naming conventions.

Step 1: Expose the business roles in S/4HANA

  1. Make sure the business roles you want to federate (e.g. SAP_BR_PURCHASER) have their launchpad spaces and pages assigned.
  2. Open transaction /UI2/CDM3_EXP_SCOPE, select the roles and choose Expose.
  3. Repeat the exposure whenever the roles, spaces or pages change, so Work Zone can pick up the updates.

Step 2: Connect S/4HANA through the Cloud Connector

  1. In the Cloud Connector, add a Cloud to On-Premise mapping to your S/4HANA system (protocol HTTPS, virtual host and port).
  2. Set Principal Type to X.509 Certificate so that principal propagation is possible.
  3. Expose the required resource paths, typically /sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/, /sap/opu/odata/, /sap/opu/odata4/, /sap/bc/ui5_ui5/ and /sap/public/bc/.
  4. Under Configuration > On Premise, create the system certificate and the CA certificate for principal propagation, and synchronize trust with your subaccount.

Step 3: Trust the Cloud Connector in S/4HANA

  1. Import the Cloud Connector CA/system certificate into the SSL server PSE in STRUST.
  2. Set the ICM profile parameters icm/HTTPS/trust_client_with_issuer and icm/HTTPS/trust_client_with_subject to the issuer and subject of the Cloud Connector system certificate, then restart the ICM.
  3. In CERTRULE, create a rule that maps the short-lived user certificate (e.g. the CN or e-mail) to the SU01 user. This is where Maria's cloud identity becomes her backend user.

Step 4: Create the destinations in the BTP subaccount

  • Design-time destination (e.g. S4H_DT😞 URL http://<virtual-host>:<port>/sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/entities, Proxy Type OnPremise, authentication with a technical user (or principal propagation), plus the property sap-client. Work Zone uses it to fetch the exposed content.
  • Runtime destination (e.g. S4H_RT😞 URL http://<virtual-host>:<port>, Proxy Type OnPremise, Authentication PrincipalPropagation, plus sap-client and HTML5.DynamicDestination = true. Apps use it when Maria opens them. Point the runtime destination for OData to the same destination unless your landscape separates them.

Step 5: Add S/4HANA as a content provider in Work Zone

  1. In the Site Manager, open the Channel Manager and choose New > Content Provider.
  2. Enter a title and an ID (e.g. s4h; this becomes the prefix of the generated role collections), and select the design-time and runtime destinations.
  3. Choose whether to include all exposed roles or only selected ones, and save. Wait until the status shows the content was fetched successfully.
  4. In the Content Manager > Content Explorer, open the provider, select the roles and choose Add to My Content.
  5. Assign the roles to your site in the Site Settings.

Step 6: Assign both keys to the user

  • Key 1 (BTP): In the BTP cockpit under Security > Role Collections, assign ~s4h_SAP_BR_PURCHASER to Maria, or better, map it to an IdP group so assignments are managed centrally in your identity provider.
  • Key 2 (S/4HANA): Make sure Maria's SU01 user exists with the same identity used in the CERTRULE mapping, and assign SAP_BR_PURCHASER in PFCG/SU01.

Quick troubleshooting checklist

  • Tile is not visible: the BTP role collection is missing, the role is not assigned to the site, or the content was not re-fetched after a change in S/4HANA.
  • Tile is visible but the app fails with 401/403: check the Cloud Connector principal propagation setup, the CERTRULE mapping and the PFCG role assignment in S/4HANA.
  • Content provider fails to fetch: test the design-time destination and check that /sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/ is exposed in the Cloud Connector.

Conclusion

You cannot replace one key with the other. Federated BTP role collections exist for operational efficiency: they bring the launchpad layout from S/4HANA into Work Zone automatically, so you do not replicate catalogs and spaces by hand. PFCG roles exist for security: they enforce the data-level authorizations in the system of record. When a user reports "I can see the tile but the app doesn't work" (or the other way around), ask which of the two keys is missing, and you will usually find the answer quickly.

In upcoming posts, I will cover other Work Zone scenarios, including apps deployed on BTP, to complete the end-to-end picture.

entry.title: Connect to AWS S3 using SAP Cloud Connector for SAP Datasphere Replication flows
entry.content:
Introduction 

When integrating SAP Datasphere with AWS S3, traffic typically traverses the public internet. While TLS encryption protects data in transit, many enterprise security policies require that sensitive data never leave the private network boundary, even when encrypted. AWS Private Link addresses this by routing S3 traffic entirely within the AWS network through a VPC Interface Endpoint, eliminating exposure to the public internet at the network layer. Combined with the SAP Cloud Connector (SCC), this enables SAP Datasphere to access S3 buckets over a SAP Cloud Connector secure TLS tunnel, without any traffic leaving the AWS backbone.

This guide walks through the setup and verification of this architecture in a lab / POC-style environment.

Disclaimer: This blog is intended for informational and knowledge-sharing purposes only. The configurations described are demonstrated in a SAP lab environment and may not reflect production-ready setups. Please refer to official AWS S3 and SAP documentation.

Architecture 

The key components are:

Component

Role

AWS S3 Bucket

Target data store; public access blocked 

VPC Interface Endpoint

Routes S3 traffic privately within the AWS network 

EC2 Instance

Hosts the SAP Cloud Connector; sits inside the VPC

SAP Cloud Connector

Bridges SAP Datasphere to the private S3 endpoint

 Prerequisites

  • An active AWS account with the VPC Interface Endpoint for S3 , allowing resources inside the VPC to reach S3 without routing traffic over the public internet.
  • AWS EC2 Instance to host the SAP Cloud Connector
  • An SAP BTP Subaccount for  SAP Datasphere (Cloud Foundry environment)

1.    Provision EC2 AWS instance 

Provision an EC2 instance inside the same VPC and subnet as the Interface Endpoint. This instance will host the SAP Cloud Connector.

Parameter

Recommended Value

Operating System

Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.x or Amazon Linux 2023

Instance Type

Medium or larger (SCC requires at least 2 vCPU / 4 GB RAM)

VPC

Same VPC as the Interface Endpoint

Subnet

Same subnet as the Interface Endpoint

Security Group

The shared security group that controls access to the endpoint; shared with the EC2 instance

Public IP

Assign a public IP for initial SSH access

2.    Verify S3 Access via Private endpoints

SSH into the EC2 instance and verify that S3 is reachable through the private endpoint.

Install AWS CLI on the Instance

ssh -i <your-key.pem> ec2-user@<instance-public-ip>

sudo dnf install -y unzip wget
mkdir -p /data/awscli && cd /data/awscli
curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o "awscliv2.zip"
unzip awscliv2.zip
./aws/install
export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/bin
aws --version

Configure Credentials and Test Access

aws configure set aws_access_key_id <YOUR_ACCESS_KEY_ID>
aws configure set aws_secret_access_key <YOUR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY>
export REGION=eu-central-1
# Test standard S3 access
aws s3 ls s3://your-bucket-name

# Test access via the PrivateLink Interface Endpoint DNS
aws s3api head-object \
  --bucket your-bucket-name \
  --key test-file.txt \
  --endpoint-url https://bucket.vpce-<endpoint-id>.s3.eu-central-1.vpce.amazonaws.com

A successful response confirms that S3 traffic is routing through the private endpoint.

3.    Install and configure SAP Cloud Connector

Download SAP Cloud Connector

Download the SAP Cloud Connector Linux Portable package from SAP Development Tools. The package is a .zip file containing an RPM installer.

Transfer the package to the EC2 instance:

scp -i <your-key.pem> sapcc-<version>-linux-x64.zip ec2-user@<instance-public-ip>:/tmp/

Install SAP Machine JRE (Java Runtime)

SCC requires Java 17 or 21. SAP Machine JRE is the recommended runtime.

wget https://github.com/SAP/SapMachine/releases/download/sapmachine-21.0.5/sapmachine-jre-21.0.5_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz
tar zxf sapmachine-jre-21.0.5_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz -C /data/
export JAVA_HOME=/data/sapmachine-jre-21.0.5
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
java -version

Install SCC

mkdir /data/sapcc && cd /data/sapcc
cp /tmp/sapcc-<version>-linux-x64.zip .
unzip sapcc-<version>-linux-x64.zip
rpm -Uvh --force com.sap.scc-ui-<version>.x86_64.rpm

Start and Access SCC

Once installed, SCC starts automatically as a service and is accessible on port 8443:

# Check service status
systemctl status scc_daemon

Open a browser and navigate to:  https://<instance-public-ip>:8443/

Log in with the default credentials and change the password immediately:

Field

Default Value

Username

Administrator

Password

Manage

4.    Connect SAP Datasphere Subaccount to SAP Cloud Connector

Set Installation Type

On first login, select Master as the installation type and save

Register the SAP Datasphere BTP Subaccount

  1. Login into your BTP Cockpit, navigate to Connectivity → Cloud Connectors → Download Authentication Data
