            You will need to upload the authenticated data file in Step 4  

     2. Login in into SAP Cloud Connector Admin UI  https://<instance-public-ip>:8443/

        Click Add Subaccount

      3. Choose to Configure using Authentication data

     4. Choose from file and browse to select the downloaded file from Step 1- Add subaccount authentication data

      5. Set Location ID you want to use and a Display Name and Finish.

      6. Verify the connection appears as active in the BTP Cockpit under Connectivity → Cloud Connectors

 

5.    Map Virtual Host to the S3 Private Endpoints

If you want to prevent your data from being routed publicly through the internet, you can use SAP Cloud Connector as a secure TLS tunnel between the customer virtual private network and SAP Datasphere to privately route the data.

Cloud Connector acts as a reverse proxy, create the following system mappings for the regional endpoints where your Amazon S3 bucket is located . you will need to map the virtual host to two separate S3 PrivateLink endpoints for CSV and Parquet files
 
1. In  SAP Cloud Connector, Select SubAccount and choose the Datasphere SubAccount

2. Go to Cloud To On-Premise and click the Add button  

    Select Non-SAP System as back-end type 

3. Set Protocol to TCP

4.  Set the internal host and port range for  Amazon S3 global endpoint for path-syle URL access (for example, s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com)

5. Set the Virtual Host and port   - must be the same as the internal host and port 

6. Click Finish to complete endpoint system mapping to enable path-style URL access

7. Add endpoint system mapping to enable virtual-hosted-style URL access. Similar to Step 2 to Step 6 

    Go to Cloud To On-Premise and click the Add button  

  • Select Non-SAP System as back-end type 

    

  • Set Protocol to HTTPS
  • Set Internal Host and Port - Internal host for Amazon S3 regional endpoint including the name of the bucket that you want to access (for example, <bucket-name>.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com)

  • Set Virtual Host and Port                      

           Hostname must be the same as the internal host and port can be different 

  • Deselect Allow Principal Propagation
  • set Host in Request Header to Internal Host

  • Click Finish to complete endpoint system mapping to enable virtual-hosted–style URL access

8. Verify the connections for both mappings in SCC

6.   Add  data source location to SAP  Datasphere

Login in SAP Datasphere and navigate to SYSTEM --> Administration

In the Data Source Configuration section add the defined SCC location to the locations list

7.    Create AWS S3 connection in SAP Datasphere using SAP Cloud Connector 

1. Login in SAP Datasphere and switch to the HANA<Space> or HDLF <space> to Create a new Connection to AWS S3 in Connection Management

2. Click Amazon Simple Storage Service connection in Connection List

3. Configure Connection parameters for Amazon Simple Storage with setting the Use Cloud Connector to True

    Make sure to select the created / corresponding Location for the  SAP Cloud Connector instance

4. Choose Next and enter connection information and click on Create Connection

5. Validate the Connection to verify the connection status 

With these steps completed, your SAP Cloud Connector is successfully installed, connected, and configured to integrate and create a native connection type of Amazon simple storage service using private endpoints with SAP Datasphere . Now in data builder , you can configure and deploy a Replication Flow with Amazon simple storage service( AWS S3) as source .

Conclusion

Setting up private connectivity between SAP Datasphere and AWS S3 is straightforward when combining AWS PrivateLink with the SAP Cloud Connector. If you want to prevent your data from being routed publicly through the internet, you can use Cloud Connector as a TLS tunnel between the customer virtual private network and SAP Datasphere to privately route the data. The setup covered in this blog walks through each layer of the architecture: provisioning an EC2 instance inside the VPC to host the SAP Cloud Connector, routing S3 traffic through a VPC Interface Endpoint, and mapping virtual hosts to the private S3 PrivateLink DNS addresses.

 

References:

SAP Cloud Connector licensing, download and installation information

Amazon Simple Storage Service Connections

entry.title: How SAP Build Work Zone Acts as Joule's Intent Solver: A Hands-On Walkthrough
entry.content:
Introduction

When a user asks Joule to "open Safety Manager", Joule doesn't decide on its own what that app is or whether the user may open it. SAP Build Work Zone's Navigation Service does that: it resolves the intent to a real, authorized launch target. In a recent project, I set this up end to end. We federated content from an on-premise SAP S/4HANA 2025 system into SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition, and I traced how a Joule request turns into an executable #SemanticObject-action intent.

What you will see, with screenshots from that work:

  • Exposing launchpad content from S/4HANA 2025 with Content Exposure v2
  • Design-time and runtime destinations through SAP Cloud Connector
  • The Content Channel settings that matter, and what to change at scale
  • Federated roles and the intents inside them, including why classic roles turn into #Shell-startGUI
  • The full path from a Joule prompt to a launched transaction

SAP's Joule setup guidance states it plainly: Joule uses the Navigation Service component of SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition, to resolve intent-based navigation targets. This post shows what that looks like in practice.

System IDs, host names and URLs in the screenshots are masked. Where an ID appears in the text, <SID> stands for the backend system ID.

The architecture in one picture

Joule understands the request, but Work Zone owns the answer to "which app, and is this user allowed?" Content reaches Work Zone through federation. The S/4HANA system exposes its roles, and Work Zone pulls them over a design-time destination through Cloud Connector.

The Navigation Service sits in the middle. If the role check fails, the intent is never returned to Joule, so the user never sees a launch card.

Step 1: Expose launchpad content from S/4HANA 2025

Work Zone can only resolve intents it knows about, so the first job is to publish the backend's roles and apps. Content federation reads them through the CDM3 service (/sap/bc/ui2/cdm3). CDM3 turns on-premise launchpad content into a standard JSON model that Work Zone understands.

On S/4HANA 2023 and 2025, exposure moved to Content Exposure version 2. In the backend I:

  1. Activated the HTTP services in SICF, including /UI2/FLP_CONTENT_EXPOSURE and the CDM3 endpoint.
  2. Allowed the services in UCON (UCON_HTTP_SERVICES / uconcockpit).
  3. Picked the roles to expose and ran the exposure (report /UI2/R_FLP_CONTENT_EXPOSURE).

Figure 1 – The content exposure HTTP service activated in SICF.

The exposure log is the proof point. It ended with "Content has been exposed and is ready to be picked up by SAP BTP."

Figure 2 – CDM3 exposure log. Roles and business apps are now available to BTP.

Tip: Activating the service only opens the door. Nothing reaches Work Zone until you actually choose the roles and run the exposure.

Step 2: Connect through Cloud Connector with two destinations

Work Zone needs two separate HTTP destinations in the BTP cockpit, both routed through SAP Cloud Connector. No backend port is exposed to the internet.

  Design-time destination Runtime destination

PurposeReads the content model (roles, catalogs, intents)Runs the apps when a user clicks or Joule launches
Used byChannel Manager, when fetching contentEnd users at runtime
AuthenticationTechnical userPrincipal propagation recommended

In Cloud Connector, I exposed /sap/bc/ui2/cdm3 with all sub-paths so the design-time destination could reach it. The runtime destination needs the additional properties that let Work Zone launch classic ABAP UIs:

Figure 3 – Runtime destination properties. sap-sysid must match the S/4HANA system ID and sap-client the target client.

What went wrong first: the initial URLs had extra path segments at the end. It worked once I removed the trailing entities from both destinations and set the runtime destination to protocol, host and port only.

Step 3: Create the Content Channel in Work Zone

In Work Zone's Channel Manager, I created a content provider that points to both destinations. This channel is what feeds the Navigation Service its intents.

Figure 4 – New content provider with the design-time and runtime destinations.

Setting What I used When to change it

Runtime destination for dynamic dataUse default runtime destinationMany live-count tiles: split that traffic onto its own destination
Content granularityRoles and related contentOlder NetWeaver or portal backends without Spaces and Pages
Automatically add all content itemsOnThousands of roles: turn it off and approve roles manually
Provision authorizations with IPSOff for the first rolloutRequired at scale, together with principal propagation
Include group and catalog assignmentsOff (S/4HANA 2025 uses Spaces and Pages)Older releases such as 1809 or 1909 that still rely on groups

After saving, the channel runs an update. Once it finishes, the backend's roles are in Work Zone.

Figure 5 – The new channel updating in Automatic Mode, next to the HTML5 Apps channel.

Step 4: Assign federated roles and inspect the intents

Federated roles arrive with a ~<SID>_ prefix, and the role is the unit of federation. Apps, catalogs and spaces sit inside their roles rather than as standalone objects. That's why Content Manager lists only roles at the top level.

Work Zone imported 59 roles and generated a matching BTP role collection for each one. Two assignments are needed before anything shows up:

  1. Assign the roles to the Work Zone site (Site Directory > Role Assignments).
  2. Assign the generated role collections to the user. Without this step, Work Zone hides the tiles even when the site has the role.

Figure 6 – Federated roles assigned to the Work Zone site.

Open any role in Content Manager and each app shows its navigation target. This is exactly what the Navigation Service hands back to Joule. A native Fiori app carries a real business intent:

Figure 7 – Role SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR_DANA: Customer Data Browser resolves to #CustomerDataPackage-preview (SAPUI5, Fiori ID F5746).

Why classic roles become #Shell-startGUI

This was the most interesting finding. The Safety Manager role (SAP_EHSM_HSS_SAFEMGR) came into Work Zone with just four apps, and none of them were business apps:

Figure 8 – Safety Manager role: the GUI launcher resolves to Shell-startGUI with parameter sap-ui2-tcode.

Checking the same role in the backend explained why. In the Launchpad Content Manager (/UI2/FLPCM_CUST), the role has zero tiles or target mappings:

Figure 9 – SAP_EHSM_HSS_SAFEMGR has no Fiori catalogs, so there are 0 target mappings.

The role is built from classic PFCG menu folders that contain SAP GUI transactions and Web Dynpro ABAP apps, not Fiori catalogs. The exposure engine can't give those their own semantic objects, so it wraps them in four generic launchers:

Work Zone app ID Inbound intent What it does

<SID>_businessapp.gui.generic#Shell-startGUIStarts any transaction in SAP GUI for HTML
<SID>_businessapp.wda.generic#Shell-startWDAStarts any Web Dynpro ABAP application
<SID>_businessapp.flp.search#Shell-searchEnterprise search on the backend
<SID>_businessapp.flp.homepage#Shell-homeReturns to the system's home page

What this means for Joule: for classic content, the intent Joule gets back is #Shell-startGUI plus a transaction code, not a business-specific intent. Authorization still applies, because the Navigation Service evaluates it against the federated Safety Manager role. A user without that role never gets the launcher.

End to end: from a Joule prompt to a running transaction

With this content in place, here is how a request like "Open Safety Manager GUI" moves through the stack. The numbers match the architecture diagram above.

  1. Prompt: the user types the request in the Joule chat.
  2. Intent extraction: Joule's language processing maps it to a target intent, #Shell-startGUI?sap-ui2-tcode=<TCODE>.
  3. Resolution in Work Zone: the Navigation Service checks the user's token (Global User ID and group claims from Cloud Identity Services). It verifies that the user has the federated Safety Manager role and, if so, returns the matching app descriptor.
  4. Navigation card: Joule shows a link to "Launch generic SAP GUI Application" with that target.
  5. Execution: the browser opens the transaction in SAP GUI for HTML on S/4HANA, through the runtime destination and Cloud Connector.

The key point is step 3. Joule contributes the language understanding, and Work Zone provides the catalog of valid, authorized targets. If the role isn't assigned, the Navigation Service drops the intent, and Joule has nothing to offer.

An earlier attempt ended here instead:

Figure 10 – A 403 when launching a Web Dynpro test app. The intent resolved, but the runtime call to the backend was refused.

Lessons learned

  • No federated role means no intent for Joule. When Joule "can't find" an app, check the user's role collections in BTP before touching Joule.
  • Expose, don't just activate. SICF and UCON only open the service. The exposure run is what publishes the roles.
  • Keep destination URLs clean. Leave trailing paths off. The runtime destination should be protocol, host and port only.
  • Open the CDM3 path in Cloud Connector, with all sub-paths, or the channel can't read content.
  • Know what your roles are made of. Classic PFCG roles give Joule generic #Shell-startGUI or #Shell-startWDA targets. Fiori-based business roles give specific intents such as #CustomerDataPackage-preview.
  • Plan for scale. Turn off auto-add for large systems, and turn on IPS provisioning with principal propagation.

Also worth knowing from SAP's Joule troubleshooting notes: if the Joule navigation button is missing, export the Navigation Service destination. Check that tokenServiceURLType is Dedicated, then refresh the content channel in Work Zone.

Wrapping up

Joule is the conversation layer, and SAP Build Work Zone's Navigation Service decides what a user can actually open. If you set up content federation carefully, Joule inherits your existing S/4HANA roles and apps as intents it can safely resolve.

Have you set up Joule with content federation from an on-premise system? I'd like to hear what you ran into, so share it in the comments.

#SAP #sapbuild #workzone Joule

entry.title: SAP Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES 15 SP6 – Part 1: Installation, BTP Connection and HTTPS Mapping
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Cloud Connector is the link between SAP BTP and the systems that stay in your own network. This series documents a Linux setup built from scratch in a lab: installation, high availability and an upgrade. Part 1 covers installing Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES 15 SP6, connecting it to a BTP subaccount and exposing an on-premise ABAP system. Part 2 adds a shadow instance, and Part 3 upgrades to 2.19.1. 

Environment

Component Version / detail
Cloud Connector2.16.2
JVMSAP JVM 8.1.112
OSSLES for SAP Applications 15 SP6
Cloud Connector VM4 GB RAM, [vCPU], 32 GB disk, on Proxmox
BackendSAP NetWeaver 7.5 ABAP, MaxDB on a separate host
BTP[trial / productive] subaccount, region [region]

Prerequisites

  • A SLES VM with static IP, working DNS and synchronized time (chronyc tracking), since clock drift breaks the connection to BTP.
  • Outbound HTTPS (443) from the VM to your BTP region, and port 8443 for the Administration UI.
  • The Cloud Connector archive and the SAP JVM RPM from tools.hana.ondemand.com.

Step 1: Install SAP JVM

 

bash
rpm -ivh sapjvm-8.1.112-linux-x64.rpm

The RPM installs to /usr/java/sapjvm_8.1.112 and creates a stable link at /opt/sapjvm_8. I point JAVA_HOME to that link, so a later JVM update does not change the path:

 
bash
cat > /etc/profile.d/sapjvm.sh <<'EOF'
export JAVA_HOME=/opt/sapjvm_8
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
EOF
source /etc/profile.d/sapjvm.sh
java -version

 

Step 2: Install Cloud Connector

 
bash
mkdir -p sapcc-2.16.2
unzip sapcc-2.16.2-linux-x64.zip -d sapcc-2.16.2
rpm -ivh sapcc-2.16.2/com.sap.scc-ui-*.rpm
systemctl enable --now scc_daemon
systemctl status scc_daemon
ss -tlnp | grep 8443

Step 3: First login

Open https://<host>:8443, log in as Administrator and change the initial password when prompted.

Default Username is Administrator and the Default Password is manage

Step 4: Create a subaccount in the SAP BTP trial

The Cloud Connector always connects to one specific subaccount, so I created a dedicated one for this lab. In the BTP Cockpit of my trial account I chose Create > Subaccount and entered [display name], [region], and [subdomain / default]. [Environment: Cloud Foundry enabled / none]. 

https://cockpit.hanatrial.ondemand.com/trial/

 

 

Once the subaccount was created, I opened its Overview page and noted two values that I need in the next step: the Subaccount ID and the region. 

 

The region matters: the Cloud Connector must be configured with the same region as the subaccount, otherwise it cannot connect.

 

 

 

Step 5: Create the system mapping to the ABAP system

The subaccount is connected, but the Cloud Connector does not expose anything yet. Every backend system has to be released explicitly through a system mapping. A mapping ties an internal host and port, which only exist inside my network, to a virtual host and port, which are the only names BTP ever sees. This keeps the real host names out of the cloud side.

In the Administration UI I opened Cloud To On-Premise, selected the Access Control tab and chose Add to start the wizard.

 

Backend type and protocol. I selected ABAP System as the backend type and HTTP as the protocol. 

 

Internal host and port. I entered the host name of my application server, nw7.sap.local, and the HTTP port of its ICM, 443. The port depends on the instance number. In transaction SMICM, under Goto > Services, you can see which ports the ICM listens on. 

 

Virtual host and port. I chose a generic virtual host, nw7.sap.local, and virtual port, 443. These values are what I will later use in the destination URL, so they should be easy to recognize and should not reveal the real system name. 

Principal type. I selected None, which means no identity is propagated from BTP to the backend. For this first test, authentication is not part of the setup. 

Remaining options. On the summary page I reviewed everything and finished the wizard. 

Exposing a resource. A new mapping exposes nothing by default. I selected the mapping and added a resource under Resources: URL path [/sap/public/ping] with the access policy [Path Only / Path and All Sub-Paths] and the resource set to active. I used this path because it is a lightweight service that needs no logon, and I checked in SICF that the service is active. 

 

Checking availability. Next to the mapping, the Check Availability button returned a green status. This check only confirms that the Cloud Connector can open a TCP connection to the internal host and port. It does not prove that the service answers, and it says nothing about whether BTP can reach it. That test comes in the next step, with a destination in the subaccount. 

Step 6: Create self-signed certificates and establish trust

The Cloud Connector and the ABAP system are separate systems, so each of them has to trust the certificate of the other. For this lab I used self-signed certificates on both sides. In production, certificates from an internal CA are the usual choice.

1. Create a self-signed certificate in the Cloud Connector

In [Configuration > On Premise > System Certificate] I chose [Create and import a self-signed certificate] and entered the host name [scc FQDN] as common name, [key size] and a validity of [period]. [SCREENSHOT: dialog] After saving, the certificate details appeared in the UI. 

 

 

2. Export it

I downloaded the certificate as a .der file , and copied it to the ABAP host:

Step 7: Secure the backend connection with the ABAP SSL server certificate

With a plain HTTP mapping, traffic between the Cloud Connector and the ABAP system is unencrypted. For HTTPS, the Cloud Connector must trust the certificate that the ICM presents. I used a self-signed certificate, which suits a lab. In production, a certificate from an internal CA is the usual choice.

1. Prepare the ABAP system

The ICM needs an HTTPS port, set in the instance profile with icm/server_port_[1] = PROT=HTTPS, PORT=443. In transaction STRUST, under SSL server Standard, I created a self-signed certificate with [nw7 FQDN] as common name. The common name matches the internal host that I use in the mapping. After saving, I restarted the ICM. 

 

2. Export the certificate

I exported the public certificate from STRUST in Base64 format. Only the public certificate leaves the system, never the PSE or a private key. To be sure that this is the certificate the ICM really presents, I compared the fingerprints from the Cloud Connector host:

 

3. Import it into the Backend Trust Store

In the Cloud Connector Administration UI, in [Configuration > On Premise > Backend Trust Store], I chose [Import Certificate] and selected the file. The certificate appeared in the list. 

 

4. Check the mapping

In Cloud To On-Premise > Access Control, in the list Mapping Virtual To Internal System, I [edited the existing mapping / added a new mapping] with protocol HTTPS, internal host [nw7 FQDN] and internal port [HTTPS port]. Then I pressed Check Availability, and the status turned green.

5. Test from BTP

The destination uses an https:// URL with the virtual host and port, Proxy Type OnPremise, and Check Connection succeeded.

 

6. Prove that the trust works

I removed the certificate from the Backend Trust Store and ran the checks again. They failed with [error]. After importing the certificate again, they succeeded. 

Conclusion

You now have a working Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES 15 SP6, running with SAP JVM 8 as a systemd service. It is connected to your SAP BTP subaccount, and it exposes your ABAP system through a system mapping that you verified from BTP with a destination and Check Connection. You also secured the backend connection: by importing the ABAP SSL server certificate into the backend trust store, the Cloud Connector now trusts the system it talks to over HTTPS.

Important Note:

This blog post demonstrates an end-to-end upgrade path and High Availability setup starting from Cloud Connector version 2.16.2 (which is the only legacy version currently available for download on the official SAP Development Tools page).

Please note that version 2.16.2 is no longer supported in production environments. If you are deploying a new Cloud Connector instance from scratch, always download and install the latest available version (2.19.1 or higher) directly.

entry.title: SAP Cloud Connector on SLES – Part 2: High Availability with a Shadow Instance and Failover Tests
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Cloud Connector is the link between SAP BTP and the systems that stay in your own network, and a single instance is a single point of failure. In Part 1 -  SAP Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES 15 SP6 – Part 1: Installation, BTP Connection and HTTPS Mapping

I installed Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES 15 SP6, connected it to a BTP subaccount and exposed an ABAP system over HTTP and HTTPS. In this part I add a shadow instance, connect it to the master and test what happens when things fail. Part 3 upgrades the landscape to 2.19.1.

A single Cloud Connector is a single point of failure for every scenario that depends on it. High availability gives you redundancy if an instance fails, and it lets you plan maintenance, such as an upgrade, by switching roles so that one instance keeps serving while you work on the other.

Environment

Component Detail
Masterscc, VM on Proxmox, Cloud Connector 2.16.2, SAP JVM 8.1.112
Shadowscc-shadow, VM on Proxmox, same versions
OSSLES for SAP Applications 15 SP6
Backend and BTPAs in Part 1: ABAP system with HTTP and HTTPS mappings, subaccount scc-lab (trial)

How master and shadow work together

The master pushes its whole configuration to the shadow during setup and sends later changes as they happen. A master can have only one shadow, and user administration is configured separately on each instance. SAP recommends placing the shadow in the same network segment as the master, but separated so that a fault on the master does not also take down the shadow. In my lab both VMs run on the same Proxmox host, so this is a functional test and not real protection against a host failure.

Step 1: Prepare the shadow VM

Before installing anything, I checked that the two VMs do not share identifying values. Run this on both servers; every value must differ:

ip link show | grep ether
cat /etc/machine-id
ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

[In my case they did not, see Troubleshooting.] I also set a static IP for the shadow, added both hosts to /etc/hosts on both servers and checked the connection in both directions:

getent hosts scc scc-shadow
nc -zv scc 8443 # from the shadow

nc -zv scc-shadow 8443 # from the master

Step 2: Install SAP JVM and Cloud Connector on the shadow

I installed SAP JVM 8.1.112 and Cloud Connector 2.16.2 exactly as described in Part 1, with the same versions as on the master. The installer found the JVM and started the daemon. I did not add a subaccount on the shadow, because the master provides the configuration.

 

Step 3: Initial setup of the shadow

At the first login I changed the Administrator password and chose Shadow (Backup Installation) as the installation type. The password of the shadow is independent from the master. After saving, the UI is titled "Cloud Connector Shadow System Administration" and shows Disconnected with a request to configure the connection to the master. 


Step 4: Enable high availability on the master

On the master, under High Availability, the status was Disabled. I pressed Enable. [What the dialog asked for]

Step 5: Connect the shadow to the master

On the shadow, in Connection To Master, I entered:

  • Master Host: scc.sap.local
  • Master Port: 8443
  • Own Host: scc-shadow.sap.local

 

and pressed Connect. The password requested here is the Administrator password of the master, not of the shadow. The status changed to Connected, and the shadow lists the master's component versions (Cloud Connector 2.16.2, SAP JVM 1.8.0_503). On the master, High Availability now shows Connected.

 

 

Step 6: Check the mirrored configuration

On the shadow, the subaccount scc-lab appeared without any manual setup. [I checked Mirrored Subaccounts, Cloud To On-Premise and Mirrored Master Configuration, and found: ...]

 

Step 7: Resilience tests

I ran three tests with the HTTP and HTTPS mappings from Part 1 in place. Because the roles change, I name both the host and its current role in each step.

Test What I did Result Time
Planned role switchSwitch roles in the High Availability screenRoles swapped, connections to the ABAP system stayed healthyAlmost instant
Loss of the shadowPowered off the VM holding the shadow roleThe active master kept serving, high availability showed Disconnected, subaccount and mappings stayed greenNo impact
Crash of the active masterImmediate power off no clean shutdownThe shadow took over as master automatically, subaccount and mappings stayed greenAbout one minute
Failed VM returnsStarted the VM againIt rejoined as shadow, high availability ConnectedAbout one minute

[BTP Check Connection (HTTP and HTTPS) after the takeover: result.] 

Planned role switch. On the instance that currently holds the master role, the High Availability screen offers the Switch roles button. I pressed it and the roles were swapped, and the connections to the ABAP system stayed healthy.

 

The shadow screen shows a check interval of 60 seconds and a takeover delay of 30 seconds. The measured time is in the same range, but I did not test other settings.

 

Troubleshooting

  1. Duplicate MAC address. Symptoms: ip neigh showed FAILED for the other VM, ping returned "Destination Host Unreachable", both VMs froze when running together, and my SSH client warned that the host key had changed. Cause: both VMs had the same MAC address. Fix: let Proxmox generate a new one for the shadow (omit the MAC):
 
bash
   qm set <vmid> --net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0,firewall=1

The interface may get a new name afterwards (for example eth2), so I renamed /etc/sysconfig/network/ifcfg-eth1 to the new name and ran wicked ifreload all.
2. Duplicate machine-id. The two servers showed the same /etc/machine-id. systemd-machine-id-setup derives the value from the VM UUID, and both VMs had the same SMBIOS UUID, so recreating it changed nothing. Fix: set a new UUID in Proxmox, then regenerate the ID:

 
bash
   qm set <vmid> --smbios1 uuid=$(cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/uuid)
   rm -f /etc/machine-id /var/lib/dbus/machine-id
   systemd-machine-id-setup
   ln -sf /etc/machine-id /var/lib/dbus/machine-id
  1. Duplicate SSH host keys. Regenerate them on the shadow:
 
bash
   rm -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*
   ssh-keygen -A
   systemctl restart sshd
  1. Host name does not resolve. SAP documents a case where the shadow shows Disconnected with an UnknownHostException because the master's host name cannot be resolved. In my case a stale line in /etc/hosts pointed the shadow's IP address at an old name. 
  2. Handshake errors. SAP also documents a case where the shadow reports that the communication with the master is not set up properly and has to be reconnected. In that case connect the shadow again. 

[Cause of the duplicate values in your lab: how the shadow VM was created.]

Conclusion

You now have a master and a shadow instance running the same version, connected and mirroring the configuration, and you have seen three situations in practice: a planned role switch, the loss of the shadow, and an unplanned crash of the master that was handled automatically in about a minute. For real protection, place the two instances on separate hosts. In Part 3 I upgrade this landscape from 2.16.2 to 2.19.1 and use Proxmox snapshots for the rollback.

entry.title: SAP Cloud Connector on SLES – Part 3: Upgrading from 2.16.2 to 2.19.1 in a High Availability Setup
entry.content:
Introduction

A Cloud Connector upgrade is a good test for a high availability setup, because it is a planned maintenance that would otherwise interrupt every connection. In Part 1 I installed Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES and exposed an ABAP system over HTTP and HTTPS, and in Part 2 I added a shadow instance and tested failover. In this part I upgrade both instances to 2.19.1 without taking the connection down.

Environment

Component Detail
Masterscc, Cloud Connector 2.16.2 → 2.19.1
Shadowscc-shadow, Cloud Connector 2.16.2 → 2.19.1
JVMSAP JVM 8.1.112
OSSLES for SAP Applications 15 SP6, VMs on Proxmox
BackendABAP system, HTTP and HTTPS mappings as in Part 1

The order of the upgrade

In a high availability setup, the shadow is upgraded first. After that, the roles are switched, so that the upgraded instance becomes the master while the former master, now the shadow, is upgraded. The installer version of Cloud Connector is upgraded in place and keeps the existing configuration, so there is no need to uninstall anything. Uninstalling and restoring a backup is not part of this procedure.

Step 1: Before the upgrade

check the current state: both instances on 2.16.2, high availability Connected, and the subaccount, HTTP and HTTPS mappings green.

take a Proxmox snapshot of both VMs

backup the configuration from the Connector screen with a password and copied the file off the server.

check the release notes of 2.19.1 for the required JVM

download the 2.19.1 archive from the SAP Development Tools site and placed it on both servers.

Step 2: Upgrade the shadow

On scc-shadow, in the shadow role:

cd /root/sapmedia
mkdir -p sapcc-2.19.1 && unzip sapcc-2.19.1-linux-x64.zip -d sapcc-2.19.1
rpm -U sapcc-2.19.1/com.sap.scc-ui-*.rpm
rpm -qa | grep -i scc
systemctl status scc_daemon --no-pager | head -5

 

The package shows version 2.19.1 and the daemon is running.

After the upgrade, my browser still showed the old interface. A hard refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R) loaded the new one. The login window looks slightly different in the new version.

 

 

 

Step 3: The mixed-version state

While the master is still on 2.16.2, the shadow shows a message that the version of the master is not up to date. This is expected. High availability stays Connected and green.

 

Step 4: Switch roles

In the High Availability screen I pressed Switch roles. The upgraded instance became the master and the former master became the shadow. I checked that everything is still healthy: the tunnel to the subaccount is connected, and the HTTP and HTTPS mappings to the ABAP backend are green (ports [80] and [443]).

 

Step 5: Upgrade the former master

On scc, now in the shadow role, I ran the same commands as in Step 2 and refreshed the browser with Ctrl+Shift+R. Both instances now run 2.19.1.

Step 6: Return to the original roles

I switched the roles back, so that scc is the master again. The shadow now reports that the master is up to date.

 

Step 7: Failover after the upgrade

I switched the roles to both servers twice, and the connection to the ABAP system was healthy each time. [Timing, and whether BTP Check Connection stayed green]

Step Instance (role) Action Result
2scc-shadow (shadow)rpm -U 2.19.1Shadow on 2.19.1, master on 2.16.2, HA green
4BothSwitch rolesUpgraded instance is master, all connections green
5scc (shadow)rpm -U 2.19.1Both on 2.19.1
6BothSwitch roles backOriginal roles, shadow reports master up to date
7BothTwo role switches in each directionHealthy each time

 

Troubleshooting

  • The UI looks unchanged after the upgrade: hard refresh the browser (Ctrl+Shift+R).
  • The shadow reports that the master is not up to date: expected until both instances run the same version.
  • If the upgrade fails: [roll back the VM to the before-upgrade snapshot, if you tested it].

Conclusion

Both instances now run 2.19.1, with the roles back in their original places and the connections healthy throughout. The high availability setup from Part 2 is what makes this possible: the shadow carries the connection while the master is upgraded, and vice versa. Both VMs run on the same Proxmox host, so this is a functional test and not protection against a host failure.

entry.title: End-to-End Principal Propagation for AI Agents with SAP Integration Suite, MCP and SAP Cloud Connect
entry.content:
A few months ago, I shared how to expose SAP Integration Suite iFlows as MCP tools so that AI agents could discover and invoke OData operations.

That PoC worked. But it left one important question unanswered:

When an AI agent calls an enterprise API, whose identity is it actually using?

My previous setup used OAuth 2.0 client_credentials: a good fit for machine-to-machine scenarios, but a technical identity is not the human talking to the agent. If every user's requests are executed under the same technical account, backend permissions and audit trails cannot automatically reflect the individual behind each request.

So I built a second PoC: SAP MCP Principal Propagation Inspector. The goal was to send a real end-user identity from an MCP client through SAP Integration Suite and SAP Cloud Connector to a non-SAP Node.js backend, and have that backend independently validate the identity and enforce its own authorizations.

The result: real end-to-end Principal Propagation, with the backend reporting VERIFIED. More importantly, it refused to return data the authenticated user was not authorized to access.

get_my_orders  |  HTTP 200  |  Principal Propagation: VERIFIED
mTLS system identity: verified
Propagated user certificate: verified
Backend role: SALES
Authorization: 0 of 4 orders visible

Four orders existed. The agent received zero. Not because the language model chose to hide them, but because the backend prevented the data from entering the agent's context.

1. Architecture: MCP, OAuth and X.509 Principal Propagation

 

The complete path looks like this:

MCP Client (Claude / MCP Inspector)
    |  OAuth 2.0 authorization_code, human user
    v
SAP Integration Suite - MCP Server (Integration Cell)
    |  BTP Destination: OnPremise + PrincipalPropagation
    v
SAP Cloud Connector
    |  1. mTLS with SCC SYSTEM certificate
    |  2. Short-lived X.509 END-USER certificate
    |     forwarded as SSL_CLIENT_CERT
    v
Node.js 22 / TypeScript / Fastify backend
    |  Verify system TLS peer BEFORE parsing user header
    |  Validate user certificate and map to principal
    |  Apply local application permissions
    v
Business API response: only authorized data

The key distinction is that two different identities must be verified:

Check Question Evidence Enforcement

SystemWhich machine is connecting?SCC system certificate presented on the TLS socketmTLS verification and peer identity pinning
End userOn whose behalf is it acting?Propagated short-lived X.509 certificateCertificate validation and backend RBAC

A certificate placed in an HTTP header is not automatically trustworthy. The backend first authenticates the transport peer. Only then does it inspect the user certificate, which is delivered through the trusted Cloud Connector path.

2. Build a non-SAP backend with authorization that the agent cannot bypass

I implemented a small REST application in Node.js 22, TypeScript and Fastify, deployed with Docker in a Proxmox homelab. SQLite stores the fictional business data; a React/Vite dashboard provides observability.

 

The MCP tool surface is intentionally small and read-only:

HTTP operation OpenAPI operationId Behavior

GET /api/meget_current_userAuthenticated identity, role and trust information
GET /api/ordersget_my_ordersOnly orders accessible to the authenticated user
GET /api/orders/{id}get_order_by_id403 for an unauthorized order; 404 if it does not exist
GET /api/reports/summaryget_sales_summaryManager-only reporting; SALES gets 403

There is no input parameter that allows the agent to choose an arbitrary user's identity. The API gets the principal exclusively from the validated certificate. Application authorization is computed on the server, not requested by the LLM.

Administrative endpoints under /api/observability/* are protected separately and are not exposed as MCP tools.

OpenAPI is the tool contract

The business-facing contract is an OpenAPI 3.0.3 document that defines the four operations, their parameters, descriptions and response types. A shortened illustration:

paths:
  /api/orders:
    get:
      operationId: get_my_orders
      summary: Get orders visible to the authenticated user
      description: Returns only orders authorized for the
        principal derived from the propagated certificate.
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Authorized orders

The description is part of what the agent sees; the actual authorization remains entirely in the backend.

3. Create the MCP Server in SAP Integration Suite

In SAP Integration Suite → Design → Integrations and APIs, I created an MCP Server artifact and selected HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification as its source type.

Setting PoC configuration

ArtifactMCP Server: MCP_PP_Inspector
RuntimeIntegration Cell
Source typeHTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification
API descriptionFour read-only business operations via OpenAPI 3.0.3
AuthenticationOAuth 2.0 / XSUAA
Authorization scopeAPI.invoke

After importing the OpenAPI contract, I verified the tools exposed by the artifact and deployed the MCP Server to the Integration Cell runtime.

Important: verify the tool names shown by Integration Suite after import. In one iteration, the generated names did not match the original OpenAPI operationId values. The names advertised by tools/list are the ones the MCP client must actually invoke.

 

4. OAuth: switch from a technical client to the actual human

My first test used client_credentials. MCP connectivity worked, but Principal Propagation failed:

The token in header 'SAP-Connectivity-Authentication'
does not contain user info and cannot be used
for Principal propagation

That token represented the technical client. There was no human principal to propagate.

For this PoC, the MCP client instead uses OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code to authenticate the real user against SAP XSUAA. The client obtains a user-context access token and uses it when invoking the MCP Server.

 

Developer Hub agent subscription

  1. Publish the MCP Server in a Developer Hub product.
  2. Create a Subscription for Agent for the specific MCP client.
  3. Choose Tenant XSUAA as the authentication provider.
  4. Enter that client's exact OAuth callback / redirect URI at subscription creation time.
  5. Configure the resulting OAuth Client ID and Secret in the MCP client; use the authorization_code flow, not a shared technical bearer token.
  6. Confirm the user receives the scope required by the MCP authorization policy.

In this scenario the MCP policy expects API.invoke. This differs from my previous Northwind iFlow PoC, where a Process Integration Runtime technical token used ESBMessaging.send.

Lesson learned: in my trial environment, editing the callback URL on an existing Developer Hub subscription did not reliably update the underlying XSUAA OAuth client. Creating a new subscription with the correct callback from the beginning was the reliable fix.

5. Configure the BTP Destination for Principal Propagation

I created a BTP Destination for the backend behind Cloud Connector:

Name=MCP_PP_BACKEND
Type=HTTP
URL=http://<virtual-host>:8443
ProxyType=OnPremise
Authentication=PrincipalPropagation
ProxyProtocol=HTTP
CloudConnectorLocationId=PVE

The three properties that matter most are:

  • ProxyType=OnPremise: the request uses SAP Cloud Connector.
  • Authentication=PrincipalPropagation: the request carries a user context that can be propagated downstream.
  • CloudConnectorLocationId=PVE: the request uses the intended Cloud Connector connection.

The Destination uses http:// for the virtual host in this tested setup. This is not the same as the internal hop to the backend: the Cloud Connector mapping explicitly enables TLS to the Node.js server.

 

6. Configure SAP Cloud Connector

I installed SAP Cloud Connector 2.19.1 in a dedicated Debian container, registered it to the BTP subaccount and configured an access-control entry for the non-SAP backend.

 

6.1 Access control and TLS

Property Configuration

Backend typeNon-SAP System
Internal hostpp-inspector.internal
Port8443
Protocol in SCC UIHTTP with Use TLS enabled
Principal typeX.509 Certificate
System Certificate for LogonEnabled
Resource exposureOnly required backend API resources

 

The backend HTTPS listener requires a trusted client certificate during the TLS handshake. A direct request without that certificate does not reach the REST application.

6.2 Two separate certificate roles

The Cloud Connector system certificate authenticates the machine to the backend over mTLS. Separately, Cloud Connector issues a short-lived end-user certificate for Principal Propagation.

I used a dedicated laboratory CA for user propagation and configured this certificate Subject Pattern:

CN=${email},OU=Propagated User,O=PP Inspector Lab,C=ES

In the tested XSUAA JWT context, ${email} resolved successfully. ${mail}, although seen in other Principal Propagation examples, was unavailable and caused certificate generation to fail.

6.3 Synchronize XSUAA trust

In Cloud Connector → subaccount → Cloud to On-Premises → Principal Propagation, I synchronized the identity provider's signing/trust information.

Without it, Cloud Connector rejected the incoming user context:

SSO token validation failed.
Make sure trust is configured correctly
in the cloud connector.

Do not confuse this with BTP Cockpit → Security → Trust Configuration. The BTP subaccount's identity trust and Cloud Connector's token-signature trust are different configuration points.

 

 

7. Backend verification: trust the connection before the header

I intentionally avoided a design that accepts any request containing an SSL_CLIENT_CERT header. Instead, the backend starts with a mutually authenticated HTTPS channel.

  1. TLS layer: require and validate the Cloud Connector client certificate.
  2. System identity: check the exact trusted identity/pin of the TLS peer.
  3. User certificate: only after transport verification, decode the propagated certificate from the trusted path.
  4. PKI checks: validate certificate signatures, trusted issuer, validity, relevant CA constraints and configured purpose policy.
  5. Authorization: map the resulting principal to a backend role and evaluate business permissions.

That order is deliberate. A valid-looking user certificate injected over an untrusted connection is rejected as TRANSPORT_NOT_VERIFIED before the backend even parses the header.

When a reverse proxy is deployed in front of the application, it must remove any client-supplied identity headers and only forward identity information from an authenticated, trusted source. Simply enabling acceptance of underscored headers is not sufficient.

DEMO and REAL_PP: no confusing simulated tests with SAP evidence

Mode Trust source Maximum verdict

DEMOLocal test CA and simulated scenariosSIMULATED
REAL_PPActual Cloud Connector mTLS + propagated user certificateVERIFIED when all checks pass

The real mode refuses to start without the required TLS material, trusted issuer configuration, administrative protection and Cloud Connector identity pin. Local simulation cannot be mislabeled as a real SAP-verified request.

8. Troubleshooting: the problems that took the most time

These are issues encountered during the actual implementation, with the fixes that worked in this laboratory environment.

8.1 OAuth invalid_client despite valid credentials

MCP Inspector initially returned 401 invalid_client / Bad credentials, while the same OAuth client worked using curl. Isolated tests showed that the authorization-code grant was enabled; the Inspector was reusing stored OAuth credentials from a previous session. Clearing the persisted credentials and using the correct subscription resolved the mismatch.

A related observation from this XSUAA environment: HTTP Basic authentication using raw client_id:client_secret worked, while a percent-encoded Basic variant returned invalid_client. This is the behavior observed for the tested client, not a claim about all XSUAA deployments.

8.2 Backend TLS hostname mismatch

SSLHandshakeException: Invalid server certificate
Peer host '192.168.1.35' does not match certificate DNS names
[pp-inspector.internal, localhost]

The backend certificate contained an IP Subject Alternative Name, but this Cloud Connector configuration rejected the connection when targeting the IP. I changed the Internal Host to pp-inspector.internal and resolved that hostname from the Cloud Connector host. Using the DNS name fixed the handshake.

To investigate the failure I also added instrumentation around Node's TLS events (secureConnection and tlsClientError), because a TCP connection alone did not prove a successful handshake.

8.3 Missing Extended Key Usage in propagated certificates

reasonCode: CERT_MISSING_CLIENT_AUTH_EKU

The local test certificates had the TLS client authentication EKU. The propagated certificates from Cloud Connector in this setup had no EKU extension. Under RFC 5280, the absence of EKU does not itself prohibit use for a particular purpose.

Rather than silently weakening validation, I made the exception explicit and tied it to a dedicated CA:

USER_CERT_REQUIRE_CLIENT_AUTH_EKU=false
USER_CERT_CA_DEDICATED=true

The application refuses to start if the first setting is disabled without the second. This design relies on an explicitly dedicated certificate-issuing authority; it should not be copied unchanged into an environment with a shared corporate CA.

8.4 Distinguished Name ordering

Node.js: C=ES, O=PP Inspector Lab, OU=Principal Propagation,
         CN=PP Inspector Lab User CA
OpenSSL: CN=PP Inspector Lab User CA,OU=Principal Propagation,
         O=PP Inspector Lab,C=ES

Plain string comparison fails even though both representations describe the same DN components. The backend canonicalizes the components for the configured issuer comparison. In a production-grade PKI validator, DN parsing and name matching deserve a standards-compliant implementation rather than naive string operations.

8.5 SSL_CLIENT_CERT disappearing at nginx

nginx may discard incoming header names containing underscores. Without the relevant configuration, the application sees CERT_HEADER_MISSING and it looks like a propagation problem.

underscores_in_headers on;

This line addresses parsing; it is not an authorization measure. Any intermediary handling propagated identity must also strip spoofable incoming identity headers and enforce the trusted TLS boundary.

8.6 Issuer allowlist containing commas

Issuer DNs naturally contain commas. My environment parser used a semicolon delimiter for the issuer allowlist. Treating commas as list separators split a valid DN into invalid fragments and rejected all user certificates.

8.7 Developer Hub callback updates

Updating a subscription callback in the Developer Hub UI did not reliably re-provision the redirect URI on the underlying XSUAA OAuth client. Creating a new client subscription with the correct callback proved more reliable than editing an existing one.

9. Real end-to-end results: the agent cannot see unauthorized data

Once the flow was running, a real MCP tool call reached the backend with a verified Cloud Connector transport and an independently validated user certificate.

HTTP status:                 200
Tool:                        get_my_orders
Principal Propagation:       VERIFIED
Transport mTLS:              VERIFIED
End-user X.509 certificate:  VERIFIED
Authenticated role:         SALES
Authorization decision:     0 of 4 orders visible
Certificate lifetime:       70 minutes (observed)

In a separate authorization comparison, I changed the backend role without changing the MCP tool, the client or the API URL:

Role evaluated by backend get_my_orders get_sales_summary

SALESOnly own authorized orders403 ROLE_INSUFFICIENT
MANAGERAll orders allowed by manager policy200 OK

Authorization happened in the backend, not inside the prompt. An agent cannot summarize or leak data that it never receives.

 

9.1 Live Demonstration: From an AI Agent Request to Backend Authorization

After getting the entire configuration working, I wanted to verify the most important part of the architecture: what actually happens when an AI agent invokes a business operation using a real user's identity?

The test follows the complete request lifecycle.

Step 1 — The AI agent invokes an MCP tool

I ask the agent to retrieve business orders. The MCP client invokes the corresponding tool exposed by SAP Integration Suite.

No user ID is passed as a tool parameter. The user's identity comes from the authenticated OAuth session.

 

 

Step 2 — The backend verifies Principal Propagation

The request travels through SAP Integration Suite and SAP Cloud Connector, where the authenticated user context is propagated as an X.509 certificate.

The backend independently verifies the Cloud Connector's system identity through mTLS and validates the propagated end-user certificate.

The observability dashboard reports:

  • Principal Propagation: VERIFIED

  • Transport mTLS: VERIFIED

  • End-user certificate: VERIFIED

  • Backend authorization: ENFORCED

Step 3 — The backend decides what the agent is allowed to see

The most interesting part happens after authentication.

A successfully authenticated user is not necessarily authorized to access every business resource.

In the tested scenario, a SALES user receives 403 ROLE_INSUFFICIENT when requesting management reports, while a MANAGER is authorized to access them.

The MCP tools, API endpoint and client remain unchanged. The authorization decision belongs entirely to the backend.

I then changed my backend role from SALES to MANAGER and repeated the exact same MCP request.

The authenticated user, OAuth session, MCP tool and SAP configuration remained unchanged. Only the role assignment in the backend was modified.

This time, the backend returned HTTP 200 with the company-wide sales report instead of HTTP 403 ROLE_INSUFFICIENT.

Same user. Same agent. Same MCP tool. Different backend permissions.

 

 

This is the key result of the PoC: the agent can request a business operation, but it cannot bypass the permissions of the authenticated human. Unauthorized data is rejected before it reaches the AI model.

 

What happened when the token expired?

I also tested an authenticated MCP session across a gap of more than eight hours. The client refreshed its OAuth token without another interactive sign-in, and the later tool invocation arrived with a different newly issued user certificate. Both invocations passed real propagation verification.

This demonstrates refresh within the tested session, not indefinite unattended access: eventually an expired or revoked refresh token may require the person to authenticate again.

10. Observability, tests and security review

I built an observability dashboard that distinguishes facts the backend can actually prove from upstream stages it cannot directly observe:

MCP Client                 NOT AVAILABLE (backend view)
SAP MCP Gateway            NOT AVAILABLE (backend view)
SAP Cloud Connector        VERIFIED
Propagated user cert       VERIFIED
Backend authorization      VERIFIED

This is deliberate. The backend cannot independently verify an upstream MCP exchange that was terminated by SAP Integration Suite, so the dashboard does not invent evidence for those earlier steps.

The PoC includes:

  • 108 automated tests using Vitest, with passing lint, typecheck and build.
  • 17/17 smoke tests against the deployed stack.
  • Two validated OpenAPI 3.0.3 specifications.
  • Contract tests checking that documented OpenAPI routes match the actual Fastify route tree in both modes.
  • Independent adversarial security review using OpenAI Codex; reported findings led to additional tests and fixes for transport trust, certificate identity matching, response disclosure and administration protection.

 

11. What this PoC does — and does not — prove

Demonstrated: real end-user identity propagated through an SAP Integration Suite MCP Server and SAP Cloud Connector into a non-SAP REST backend, followed by cryptographic certificate checks and backend-enforced role authorization. Token refresh was observed across a prolonged authenticated session.

Not demonstrated: deployment against S/4HANA/ABAP, production hardening, load testing at scale, or write operations. The environment used SAP BTP Trial and a Proxmox homelab, and the business dataset was fictional.

The backend certificate-chain checker also does not claim to be a complete RFC 5280 implementation. It does not enforce every path-length, name-constraint, certificate-policy or algorithm-policy rule, and it does not perform CRL/OCSP revocation checking. Those are real limits and must be addressed before adopting this pattern as a production security component.

12. Final thoughts

My first MCP PoC answered:

Can AI agents discover and invoke enterprise APIs through SAP Integration Suite?

This second experiment answers a harder question:

Can the backend enforce the permissions of the actual human behind the agent?

In this tested environment, yes. XSUAA authenticated the user, SAP Integration Suite exposed the MCP tools, Cloud Connector propagated the identity, and the backend independently checked the trust boundary before deciding which business data to return.

The most important result was not the successful 200 OK. It was the data that never reached the AI agent.

Related reading: From SAP Integration Suite iFlow to MCP Tools: Exposing OData APIs to AI Agents (my earlier PoC).

Technologies: SAP Integration Suite, SAP BTP, SAP Cloud Connector, MCP, XSUAA, OAuth 2.0, X.509, Node.js, Fastify, TypeScript, Proxmox.
